How can this eBook help improve sales operations and ease the burden of paperwork?: Too often, finalising a sale can turn into a time-consuming nightmare full of tedious paperwork. After the verbal yes, sales reps and operations folks spend several days formalizing and completing the order. It makes for a bad experience on both the customer and company sides.
Download this eBook to learn how you can improve your sales operations and finally get some sleep.
completion:
The promise in that blurb is worth having. A deal that drags on for days after the customer has said yes loses something on both sides. The buyer waits for what he ordered, and the seller carries the risk that someone will back out while everyone is busy with forms. A good deal of that delay is usually paper. It is mostly copy, a signature here and there, a form that has to be filled in again because nobody checked it first. If your book shows people how to get rid of that, it will help them, and they will be glad of it.

The other promise is not so clear, and the blurb does not say how much of it is true. How much of the paperwork is a machine error, and how much is a person working slowly or carelessly? If most of it is the first, the book will earn its title. If much of it is the second, a machine will not fix it, though it might show who is behind.

As for the sleep, that is a smaller claim, and I am fairly sure of it. Sales and operations people who are tired and annoyed at four in the afternoon are more likely to make mistakes at five. If your book cuts the errors, it will also cut some of the overtime, and some of the lost sleep. I would not lean on that too hard, though. Sales people who have been in the job for years will know that some of their paperwork exists so that someone can come back later and say the deal was never confirmed. A book that treats every form as a burden will annoy the very people whose help it needs. The best ones show readers how to stop doing the work that nobody really needs.

prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from field workers who watched wild groups for years, and from a few trained monkeys who learned to use signs or buttons. The picture is patchy, because comparing one species with another is hard. Monkeys differ a great deal in size, in how they live, and in how much of their lives they spend in trees.

What seems to happen across many species is this. When a monkey finds a good patch of fruit, or a place where the insects are thick, it often calls the others. It calls them to the food, and it also tells them what kind of food it is. A call that means "food here" can still carry a message about what the food is like.

They also seem to pass on something like what to eat. Young monkeys learn a great deal by watching which plants the adults eat and which ones they pass by. You could call that a kind of talk about food, though no one has shown that they do it on purpose.

They tell each other where the food is. How precise that information is differs a lot from one species to another.

And they appear to know something of each other's wants. A monkey will often give up a share of its food to another who looks as though it needs some.

Some of this I hold as fairly sure, especially the basics. Much of the detail, especially how much meaning a call carries, is still argued over.

Where did you have in mind? A particular species, or a place where two kinds of monkey meet?

What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
Start small and attach the practice to something you already do. Most people who keep a practice have one simple rule for it: it has to take less than five minutes, and it has to be somewhere comfortable.

Some ways to fit it in:

- After brushing your teeth in the morning, sit on the edge of the bed and breathe slowly for a minute.
- At lunch, eat one sandwich without the phone.
- Before you start the car in the evening, put one hand on the steering wheel and feel it for three breaths.
- Before bed, lie on your back with your feet up against the wall and just breathe.

If you have a few minutes, try this. Sit or lie somewhere comfortable. Close your eyes or lower your gaze. Breathe in through your nose for four counts, out for six. When your mind wanders, notice where it went and come back to the breath. Five minutes is enough.

For optimal benefits, research on mindfulness and relaxation is fairly consistent about dose. The strongest evidence for lasting effects, on stress, anxiety and pain, comes from programmes like MBSR, which give people about 45 minutes a day of formal practice, six days a week, over eight weeks. That is a lot, and it works for some people.

For most people the useful figure is smaller. About 10 to 20 minutes a day, most days, produces measurable gains in attention, emotional regulation and stress resilience within a few weeks. Consistency matters more than length. Fifteen minutes every day beats two hours on Sunday.

As you get better at it, you can stretch it. A ten-minute practice can become twenty, or you can add a second session. The person who has done this for years will tell you the practice grew by small amounts, and that the small amounts were the ones that stuck.

One thing to keep in mind. Relaxation can calm the body quickly, but it does not always change what you are attached to. If you want something that changes both, add one short reflection each day. Ask what you were holding onto today, and let it go.

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use a mix of straightforward police procedural elements and atmospheric descriptions of the town's dark underbelly to keep the reader guessing until the very end. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. Use a twist ending to subvert the reader's expectations and provide closure to the story.
completion:
The rain in Oakhaven didn't fall so much as hang in the air, a drizzle that came up from the river and settled in the wool of your coat.

Detective Inspector Mara Kowalski knew every bridge in town. She knew which ones the fishermen used and which ones the teenagers used for jumping. She knew which ones had been painted with slogans no wash ever took off.

The fourth body had been found at half past six that morning. A young woman, dressed in her best clothes, seated on a park bench under a willow, with her hands folded in her lap as though she were waiting for someone. The coroner would say the time of death was somewhere between midnight and three in the morning. Mara knew better, because she had stood at that bench at half past two, and the body had already been cold.

She had spoken to no one about that.

The first murder had been a year ago, two days before Christmas, in the same park, the same willow, the same folding of the hands. The girl that time had been nineteen, a nursing student named Priya Nair, who had been walking home from her shift at the hospital. The case had gone cold within a month. The man who had led it had left the force six months later, and Mara had heard him say once, at a funeral, that some streets in Oakhaven you could walk down in daylight and still come out wrong.

Now the second case had gone to a young officer with a laptop and a quota, and the first case file sat in a cabinet in the basement, marked for review.

Mara turned her collar up against the drizzle and walked to the cordon.

"You shouldn't be here," said the young officer. "The family's lawyer is on the way."

"Then I'd better hurry."

"You have no jurisdiction."

"I have a badge and a car." She looked at the bench. "And I've been waiting a year to sit down here."

She sat. The wood was damp through her trousers.

The town had a way of making its secrets public. The gossip in the tea shops was often better than the police report. That morning the whole of Oakhaven knew that Kowalski was back on the willow case. They knew it because she had been seen at the fourth scene before anyone had been allowed near it, and because she had not taken the car.

She knew who had let it out. She had been at the pub last night, the same pub every night for a month, and she had spoken the case aloud to someone. She could not remember who.

The person she most wanted to see was already there.

Dr. Anjali Mehta was sitting in her surgery when the inspector came in without knocking. That was fine. Anjali was used to it.

"The fourth one," Mara said. "Same M. Same bench. Same hands."

"Same hands," Anjali agreed. She did not look up from the chart. "You know what that means, and you know I can't tell you more than I've told you."

"A pattern. A man is learning."

"A pattern is a story people tell themselves about five deaths. It may be true. I have seen the photographs. I have seen nothing that points to one man."

"It points to him."

"Who?"

Mara did not answer.

"You came to me about a year ago," Anjali said. "About the first case. You asked me things I would not answer. You have come back every month since, and each time you ask smaller questions and think you are asking larger ones."

"Did you find anything?"

"I found what I found. It went into the file. The file has been sitting in a basement for a year."

"Who put it there?"

Anjali closed the chart. "You should ask the person who opened it."

The person who had opened it was Constable Tomasz Okafor, and he was standing at the counter in the basement with a cup of tea someone had made for him and looked as though he would like to throw it out.

"The review," he said. "I was asked to re-examine the Nair file."

"By whom?"

"He didn't say. Someone upstairs."

"Did you find anything?"

"No." He looked at her. "I think I should have found something. I am new. Maybe I am just blind."

"There is a box in the evidence locker that does not appear on the inventory."

Tomasz went still, the way a man goes still when he hears a floorboard creak in a house he has just been told is haunted.

"How do you know that?"

"Does it exist?"

"It exists. I have never been allowed to open it."

"Why not?"

"That is for someone else to decide."

Mara looked at him for a long moment. She believed him, and she did not believe him, and she could not tell which.

"I am going to the locker," she said.

"Ma'am."

"Stay out of it."

She did not go to the locker. She went home, and she sat at her kitchen table with the case file open in front of her, and she read the interview with the man they had questioned in the first week. He had been a landscaper who had worked in the park. He had been questioned for three hours. He had been released. There was a line in the transcript that she had read twelve times and never understood.

"He knew I was coming," the man had said.

Mara had read it as a psychopath's boast. Now she read it as a frightened man saying something true.

She got up and put on her coat.

The man's name was Reginald Moss. He ran a landscaping business, and he had two greenhouses at the end of the road behind his house, and he was growing orchids in the winter, which was not something you did unless you had a great deal of patience or a great deal of money. He opened the door himself. He was a small man with kindly eyes and hands that had clearly done a great deal of growing.

"I heard you were asking about the park," he said. "I heard a great deal."

"About the first girl. Priya. Did you see her in the park that night?"

"I told the police. I told them everything."

"You told them something, and you told them something else. You said, 'He knew I was coming.' I always thought you meant the killer knew you were coming. I think you meant something else."

He looked at her for a long time. "That night I was working late in the second greenhouse. I heard footsteps on the gravel, and I knew them. Not the man you are looking for. A man who walks the perimeter every evening at half past two. He has done it for eight years. He walks it in the rain."

"Who?"

"I don't know his name. I have never seen his face. But he talks to the birds."

The man at the bench that night had been watching the park. He had been watching for someone, or he had been watching to make sure no one was watching him.

Mara left without telling him she believed him. She drove straight to the river.

The man she had spoken to in the pub was standing on the first bridge, the one by the old mill, looking down at the water. He was wearing the grey coat she had seen him in three nights running.

"I have been waiting for you," he said.

"Did you know he was coming?"

"He comes every night. He walks the edges. He has never gone into the park."

"Then what did you mean?"

The man smiled, and it was a sad smile. "I meant that I knew you were coming. You come to me every night, and you think you are buying me a round. You asked me about the park three nights ago, and you asked me a great deal of it. I told you what I knew, and I told you what I didn't know, and you walked out without paying."

"You knew about the box."

"I know a great deal, Inspector. Most of what I know is worth nothing to anyone. Some of it is worth something to you. The man who walks the perimeter stopped walking it six months ago."

"Why?"

"His wife died. In March."

Mara felt the table in her kitchen come up under her, the way you feel a car going over a bump in the dark.

"The review," she said. "Okafor's review. It was meant to clear the file."

"Yes."

"Who sent him?"

"He will tell you. I have never asked him."

"Then why tell me any of this?"

"Because you sit on that bench in the rain and talk to a corpse, and you think no one sees you do it. They see it. Some of them have been trying to get you to stop for a year. You answer every one of their letters the same way. You write that you are fine. You are not fine. I would like to think that matters to you. It probably does not matter to the next girl on that bench."

"You knew about the third one before it happened."

"I knew about the second one before it happened. I told someone. They did nothing. I will not pretend I did more than I did."

"Was it him? The man at the bench? Or was it you?"

He did not answer for a long time.

"I will tell you one thing," he said. "Look at the fourth girl's phone records. Look at who she was calling in the week before she died. I think you will find the same number there that Priya was calling."

Then he walked off the bridge and into the fog, and she did not call him back. She had no reason to, and she was not sure she had heard him correctly.

In the morning she went through the phone records. There was a number that came up in both files. It belonged to a call centre in the city, and it belonged to the man who had opened the review.

She sat at her desk with the file open in front of her.

The inspector who had opened the review was her old partner. He had been the one to tell her to step back from the case a year ago, in that same kitchen, with a tray of tea. He had told her she was not well enough to work it. She had thought then that he was looking out for her, and she had not been sure.

Now she was less sure.

He had sent a young officer to close her case. He had opened a box she could not get at, and she had asked the one person in town who might know what was in it, and he had told her to look at the fourth girl's phone.

She could not tell which of those he had done for her and which for himself. She did not think he would know either. Men who love someone and want to control what happens to her usually cannot tell the two apart themselves.

She wrote the review herself. It went to the chief, to the review board, and to the family. It said what she knew and how she knew it, and it said what she did not know, and it said whose case it was and whose it was not. Then she wrote out her resignation, and she read it twice before she signed it.

She left the box in the cabinet. Someone with the authority to open it should open it, in the open, with the family's lawyer sitting there. She had spent a year wanting to be the one who opened it. That was the part of the case she was letting go of, and it was the part that had been hers all along.

At half past two she went out and walked to the park. She sat on the bench under the willow. It was dry. No one had sat there since the fourth girl.

The man came along the edge of the park, as he had done for eight years, and stood at the path where she could see him. He was wearing a good coat and a hat. He did not sit down. He looked at the bench for a long time, and then he walked on, around the far side of the lake, the long way.

Mara sat there until it grew dark. She did not call him back, and she did not follow him. She thought he might come back tomorrow. She thought he might not.

There was a fifth body, she knew that much. Whether it would be on a bench under a willow, with its hands folded, she did not know, and neither did he. What she could do was sit there in the daylight, and write things down, and hand them to someone with the power to act on them. That was a smaller thing than the case. It was still something, and for the first time in a year it was hers.

prompt: Write a program using Python that reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file and outputs the data in a formatted table. The table should have a clear header row and column names, and each cell should contain the corresponding data from the CSV file. The output should be visually organized and easy to read. Ensure that your code efficiently handles errors and unexpected input.
completion:
Here's a program that does that. It uses only the standard library, so you don't need to install anything extra.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read a CSV file and print it as a formatted table."""

import csv
import sys
import textwrap


def format_table(rows, header=None, width=None):
    """Format rows of data into a table.

    Each cell gets a fixed width, chosen from the widest entry in its column:
    the header, any row, or the default minimum. Text that is too long
    gets wrapped onto a second line, indented so the columns stay aligned.
    """
    if not rows:
        print("No data to display.")
        return

    if width is None:
        width = [20] * len(rows[0])

    def cell(text, col):
        text = str(text).replace("\n", " ")
        if len(text) > width[col]:
            lines = textwrap.wrap(text, width=width[col], break_long_words=False)
            text = "\n".join(lines)
        return text.ljust(width[col])

    def line():
        return "+".join("-" * w for w in width) + "+"

    if header:
        print(line())
        print("|" + "|".join(cell(h, i) for i, h in enumerate(header)) + "|")
        print(line())

    for row in rows:
        print("|" + "|".join(cell(row[i] if i < len(row) else "", i) for i in range(len(width))) + "|")

    print(line())


def read_csv(path):
    """Read a CSV file and yield (header, rows) as plain strings.

    Empty lines and lines that are only whitespace are skipped.
    Rows that have fewer columns than the header are padded with blanks.
    Rows that have more are cut to fit.
    """
    try:
        file = open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8")
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"Cannot open '{path}': {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return

    with file:
        reader = csv.reader(file)

        # Find the first non-empty row to use as header
        header = None
        rows = []

        for raw in reader:
            text = " ".join(raw)
            if text.strip():
                if header is None:
                    header = [c.strip() for c in raw]
                else:
                    row = [c.strip() for c in raw]
                    if header and len(row) != len(header):
                        row = row[: len(header)] if len(row) > len(header) else row + [""] * (len(header) - len(row))
                    rows.append(row)

        if header is None:
            print("The file contains no data.", file=sys.stderr)
            return

        yield header, rows


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("Usage: python table.py <file.csv>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    path = sys.argv[1]

    try:
        header, rows = next(read_csv(path))
    except StopIteration:
        sys.exit(0)

    format_table(rows, header=header)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

To run it:

```
python table.py data.csv
```

The program reads the file, skips blank lines, trims each cell, and builds a grid with a header row on top. Every column is as wide as its widest entry, so the table never looks cramped and never spills over. If a cell is too long, it wraps onto a second line, and the indentation keeps the columns lined up. The borders come from the same character everywhere, with gaps between columns, so it looks like a table and isn't just a block of text.

It handles a missing or unreadable file, a file with no data, headers that don't match the row lengths, and extra columns. Bad data goes to standard error, and the program leaves a normal exit code alone.

There is one thing to know. The program assumes the first non-empty line is the header. If your file has a title line above the column names, that line becomes the header, and the real column names get printed as the first row of data. Most CSV files don't have that, but it is worth checking.

If you would rather not type the borders yourself, the third-party library tabulate does the same job: `pip install tabulate`, then `print(tabulate(rows, headers=header))`. The version above needs no installation.

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 2:14 in the morning, in the basement of the Kiran Institute for Atmospheric Physics. Dr. Adeyemi's students called the substance blue ice, because it was a crystalline gel that stayed at a temperature no probe could read and gave off a light like deep water.

Adeyemi was mixing it for the third time that night. The mixture went wrong the way mixtures sometimes do. A pressure spike, a vent that wouldn't close, and a boy of twenty-one, Kofi, who had no business being alone in the lab, holding the lid shut against the vent so the others could get out. Adeyemi came back for him and found him on the floor, the gel in his hair and down his neck.

He didn't burn. He absorbed it.

Adeyemi carried him out on a gurney. He was dead by the time they reached the ward, and she was not sure he was dead when she left him.

That was the first thing she noticed the next morning. She couldn't read his temperature with the probes, and she couldn't read it with her own hands either.

The second thing was the light in her arms.

It came on at 6:40, when a nurse turned on the ward's fluorescent lights too quickly. Her veins showed through her skin as a map of blue, and the lights went out for good. The backup lamps came on, and then she turned her hands over and they went out too.

She sat very still in the hospital bed and let the dark come. She was a scientist. She knew what she had been exposed to, and she knew what she knew. She didn't know what she was.

The third thing was that some of her memory of the night was Kofi's. She knew his mother's telephone number the way she knew her own. She knew the route he walked to the lab, and why he took the long way. She had never met his mother.

She didn't try the hospital's telephone. She used her phone and called it herself. A woman answered on the second ring, and Adeyemi understood everything at once, the blue ice, the gel, why the boy had been in that lab at two in the morning. The woman said Kofi had been working on the gel for his final project. He was going to use it for clean water in villages that had no pumps.

Then Adeyemi asked the question she'd been dreading. Did he suffer?

There was a long pause. The woman said he had been afraid, and then he had been calm. She said it very carefully, and Adeyemi understood that she didn't know.

She hung up and lay there with her eyes open until the light came back into the ward.

For the next week she did two things. She kept the recordings from the accident, all of them, including the ones that made her look careless. And she worked out, on paper, what she had felt.

The feeling had two sides. There was the cold and the dark, which she could hold like a stone in her palm. And further out there was the whole building, the air in it, the water in the pipes, the heat in the walls, which she could feel the way she could feel Kofi's calm. She found that she could hold both at once. That frightened her more than either one.

She told no one, not Adeyemi, though he came every day and brought her the readings from his own instruments, which showed nothing at all. She couldn't tell him. She didn't know what she would do with it. Nobody knew yet, not even the people who study what happens to a person when he gains a power like hers.

On the fifth day the building's safety system went off in the east wing. A solvent tank had ruptured, and the alarms were already sounding. Most of the staff were clearing the building. Adeyemi was still in the stairwell.

She didn't think. She put her hand flat on the concrete wall and felt the solvent moving through the floor drains, and she closed her hand.

The flow stopped in its tracks, a gallon a minute held still as a fish in ice. She held it for about four seconds. Then she let it go, slowly, because she wasn't sure how much it needed to move.

The fire team came up from the basement and found a woman sitting on a step with her eyes closed. They found her again three days later, in the same place, holding a pressure reading at zero so that no one would open a valve near her.

On the tenth day Adeyemi came to her with a file.

"The institute is going to shut the ice program down," he said. "Tomorrow. All of it. They're calling it a precaution."

"They don't know what it does to a person," she said.

"No. Nobody does. That's exactly why we should keep it running, under people who watch each other. A program nobody watches is the danger. I've asked for a review. I think you should ask for it too, in your own name."

She thought about it. She could be gone by morning. She could go somewhere nobody could find her, and hold a city's power grid at zero if anyone ever came looking. Nobody could watch her from outside if there was nobody outside.

She said she'd write the proposal. She said she couldn't promise anything else.

He didn't ask for more. He told her about the review, and about the water project Kofi had been working on, and she listened.

She hasn't decided yet. Some nights she practices on a single lightbulb, turning it from white to blue and back again, and other nights she doesn't touch anything at all. She is still keeping the recordings. She is still writing down what she feels, Kofi's memories included, because she isn't sure how much of them is his and how much of them is hers.

There is one person she can tell, and she has told him nothing yet. The review will need someone to watch the subjects, and Adeyemi means to ask her. She will have to decide whether to say yes before the proposal is signed. She has three days.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness at Work: Practical Benefits for Employees and Employers

In an office where a colleague has just sent an email saying "we need to talk," most people feel their heart rate rise before they have read a word. They are not weak. They are reacting to a signal their bodies learned to read long before there were offices. Mindfulness is the practice of noticing what is happening in the body and the mind as it happens, without immediately acting on it. In the workplace this does not mean becoming calm about everything. It means that between a trigger and a reaction there is room to choose how to respond.

The benefits are not only a matter of feeling better. Research on attention suggests that people lose a large share of their working day to distraction. A widely cited study found that workers checked email or instant messages every few minutes, and that it took a substantial amount of time to get back to the task they had been doing (Mark, Gudith and Klock, 2008). Mindfulness trains attention, and in trials where participants practised a brief daily meditation, researchers found improvements in attention, memory and reasoning, along with fewer negative moods (Jha, Crouch, Lampinen and Loewenstein, 2010). For an employee this could mean finishing a report before lunch instead of at seven at night. For the employer it means work that is done well and a person who comes back next week.

Mindfulness also helps with stress, and the evidence for that is strong. A review of many studies concluded that mindfulness programmes produced moderate reductions in anxiety, depression and pain, and that these gains tended to last over time (Goyal et al., 2014). People who are less stressed make better decisions, get along better with colleagues, and are less likely to burn out.

Practising mindfulness at work does not require a retreat. Some things can be done individually. When an email makes you reach for a reply, stop, take one slow breath, and read the message again. The breath takes fifteen seconds. The reply may well be different. Set a timer for five minutes once or twice a day and sit without a screen. You will lose some minutes. You will get back more than you lose. Eat one meal a day without looking at anything else. When you are in a meeting and feel yourself getting heated, notice your body before you speak. Notice the tightness in your chest, the heat in your face, the sentence you are about to say. Then say it, or leave it alone.

Management can do more than allow this. The first thing a manager can do is notice their own reactions. If the manager answers every message at once, the whole team learns that this is the job. If the manager takes a break in front of others, they make it acceptable. Beyond that, short practices can be built into ordinary work. A meeting can begin with one minute of silence. A team can agree on a rule that messages do not have to be answered within the hour. Companies can offer sessions led by a trained teacher, because a good teacher is worth more than any app. They can also look at the hours. Much of what wears people out is not stress but too many hours.

One thing is worth saying plainly. Mindfulness works best when the conditions that wear people out are also being addressed. If an office is short of staff, no amount of breathing will fix it, and telling people to be more mindful can become a way of leaving that problem alone. Used properly, mindfulness gives people the space to see what is actually going on, including what is going wrong, and to do something about it.

The research is promising, and much of it comes from short trials. It is not a cure for everything, and it works best as part of a decent and fairly run workplace.

References

Goyal, M., Singh, S., Sibinga, E. M. S., Gould, N. F., Loannidis, J. P. A., Depp, C. and Doherty, J. (2014) 'Meditation programmes for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis', JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(3), pp. 357 to 368.

Jha, A. P., Crouch, J. A., Lampinen, T. M. and Loewenstein, G. (2010) 'Aiding and abetting: the effects of mindfulness training on prosocial behavior', in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 107(43), pp. 18,322 to 18,327.

Mark, G., Gudith, D. and Klock, U. (2008) 'The cost of interrupted work: more time to get back', in Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 169 to 178.

The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery list. Elena had written it on the back of a shopping bag in marker, with arrows and a question mark where the road turned.

They left the valley at first light. There were four of them. Elena, who had spent twenty years as a nurse in a county hospital and still carried the habit of checking pulses. Kofi, a former mechanic with easy hands and a hard time trusting anyone. Miko, seventeen, small, quick, and the only one of the four who knew which way north was. And old Hal, who had carried the water filter since the first week and said nothing at all.

The highway was closed at the first overpass. A semi had gone through the guardrail and settled across the lanes, and someone had written KEEP GOING in red paint under it. Kofi looked at the truck for a long time.

"I'd like to get under that," he said. "I think I can get under it."

"You can," said Miko. "The question is whether you want to come out the other side."

They went around instead, through the switchbacks of the old state road, and spent the morning climbing. By noon the heat had settled on them like a blanket. The dry grass gave up its last green in the middle of the afternoon, and they walked through it in silence.

Elena went first. She stopped at the ridge and held up a fist, the way she had when she worked nights and the ward was quiet.

"There's smoke," she said. "Two places. One's too close."

Kofi looked through the binoculars. "A campfire. Someone's cooking."

"A farm," said Miko. "I know that farm. They had a orchard before the blight. And there's a windmill."

The windmill was turning, slowly, against a sky that was going gray. Down in the draw there was a house with its porch lights on. Four windows, four lights, in a county that hadn't had power for three years.

They came down off the ridge without a word. They came in from the back, because Miko said so, and Elena noticed that she didn't argue. Kofi went first with the flashlight, and he swept the yard slowly, the way you'd sweep a dark garage for a cat.

Nobody was in the yard.

The porch creaked under them. Inside, the house was cold and tidy, and there was food on the table: jars on a shelf, a bag of rice, a tin of something with a label still on it. Someone had drawn a circle in chalk on the kitchen floor.

Elena looked at it for a long time. "They left," she said. "They left in a hurry. Look at the stove."

The stove was still warm.

Upstairs there were three bedrooms. Two had beds. The third had a mattress on the floor and a board across the window, with a line of small stones on the sill. Miko went to it and looked out.

"Road," she said. "And the creek. They could see anyone coming."

"You think they made it?" asked Kofi.

Miko didn't answer. She turned the board over and looked at it from every angle, and then she put her finger to her lips and pointed down at the yard.

Through the window they could see two figures coming up the drive. They weren't running. They were walking carefully, the way people walk when there might be a trap. One of them had something on his shoulder that looked like a rifle.

Kofi reached for the shotgun in the hall closet and Elena caught his wrist. Not hard. He looked at her, and she didn't let go.

"Wait," she said. "Wait and watch. That's an order."

She was a nurse. She couldn't make him listen. But Kofi stood still, and he wasn't the only one.

The two came into the yard and stopped under the windmill. They looked up at the house, and they didn't go inside. One of them called out something. From that far away it was impossible to hear, but Miko knew their faces.

"They're hungry," she said. "And they're afraid of us."

Elena went out the front door alone, with her hands open and visible, the way you'd approach a dog that might bite. Kofi followed halfway and stopped at the porch step.

"Ask them," Elena said. "Ask them about the road."

The man with the rifle didn't lower it. "You took our well," he said. "You've been at our water all week."

"We didn't know it was yours," said Elena. "We've been walking since this morning. We'd heard your fire and we came to say sorry."

He looked at her for a moment, and then he looked past her at the house, at the lights, at the food on the table.

"There are four of you," he said. "And you're all standing still."

"There are four of us," said Elena. "If you want to check us, check us."

They checked them. Not very thoroughly. Kofi laughed at something the woman said, a low laugh, and then he was quiet again.

They talked for a long time in that yard, under the windmill, with the door of the house standing open behind them. Inside, Miko sat on the third mattress and listened. She couldn't hear every word. She heard enough.

The man's name was Duane. The woman's was Priscilla. They had a daughter, nine, who was asleep upstairs. Their farm was two days east, up the creek. The road was closed at the overpass, but there was a ford further up that worked in dry weather. This week it was dry. They had seen the four-wheeler tracks in the mud.

"They saw us leave," said Priscilla. "This morning. When we went to check the wells."

Miko understood then what the stones on the sill were for. Someone had been counting days.

Elena came inside and sat down on the floor beside her.

"Any good?" she asked.

"They watched us go," said Miko. "All four of us. And then they left their own water and came looking for us."

"They're scared," said Elena. "Of people like us, walking around with guns."

"I'm scared of people like us," said Miko.

Elena didn't argue. She sat there a long while in the dark, and then she got up and went out to help with the dishes.

They ate at the table with the man and the woman. Hal sat in the corner with his back to the wall, and he ate everything on his plate. Nobody asked him why. Afterward, in the yard, he pulled Elena aside.

"I know what you're thinking," he said. "You're thinking about the ford."

"I'm thinking about it," she said.

"You could take them," said Hal. "You could take them to the ford and leave them there. Four people against two, in the dark."

"They have a daughter," said Elena. "And they watched us leave."

"And if they turn around on us in the morning?"

Elena thought about it for a long time. She didn't know. Nobody in that yard knew.

"Then we'll know in the morning," she said. "We'll know in the morning."

They left at first light. The ford was where Miko said it would be, and it was dry. Duane went first on the four-wheeler, and Priscilla went last with the rifle on her lap. Kofi watched them go, and he didn't say anything.

They didn't know if it was a trap. Maybe it was. They would find out in a few days, if they lived.

The destination was a place a relief team had mentioned, a town a few hundred miles north with a generator and a hospital and a fence. Nobody knew if it still had a fence.

Elena walked most of the way. She thought about the house on the way, the porch lights, the chalk on the floor, and about the two people going back to a dry well. She thought about it every day for a long time afterward. She never quite worked out whether they had made a mistake or a promise. She decided it didn't matter which. What mattered was that when they reached the town, whoever was running it would find four people who knew how to keep a house, and that there would be food on the table for whoever came after them.

Halfway there Kofi fell off the four-wheeler and broke his ankle. Elena set it in the back of a pickup, and they walked the rest of the way.

The town was smaller than they had hoped. The generator ran on a schedule. The hospital was half empty, which was better than nothing, and the fence was real.

They got in. Duane and Priscilla got in the next week, on a road nobody had told Elena about. They didn't hug. They stood in the kitchen of the relief compound and looked at each other for a while, and then Priscilla asked Kofi whether he knew anything about windmills.

The story of that journey got told there in bits. Some parts came out wrong, the way stories do. Someone said the four had fought the two at the ford. Someone else said the two had tried to rob the four and been caught. Elena listened to both and said nothing. She went out and checked the well. It was dry. She didn't say anything about that either.

She thought about it for a while. The dry well was real, and it wasn't in any story anyone was telling.

There was a freezer in the basement of the compound, and someone had written KEEP OUT in marker on a grocery bag taped to it. Elena looked at the bag for a long time. Then she wrote on a second bag, in the same marker, and stuck it over the first.

THEY SAID ASK FIRST. THERE'S FOOD IN HERE FOR WHOMEVER COMES AFTER.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. completion:
I have led teams through hard moments more than I have been the one giving the orders. Most of what I know about leading comes from watching the people I worked with, and from the times I led badly. One incident stands out. It is about a night shift at a hospital, and it is about a man who was not yet a doctor.

The night was the first I had spent in the emergency department of a small district hospital. At half past two in the morning a man was brought in with a wound in his thigh. The blood vessels there are large, and this one had been cut close to where a large vessel runs. The wound was packed, the patient was on fluids, and his blood pressure was holding. What was not settled was whether a surgeon could reach the hospital by morning.

I was the senior nurse on the ward. My job that night was the team, the ward, and the machines. I had three others with me. There was Priya, a registered nurse who had worked there for nine years and knew every nurse on the roster. There was Tunde, a medical student on his first emergency rotation, whose hands were steady and whose face showed it. And there was Okafor, who had been a nurse for twenty years before he retired, sat on the ward that night, and had never once been asked what he thought.

The hospital had no surgeon on call. The nearest one was at a teaching hospital ninety minutes away by road. The road might be bad.

The first thing I wanted to know was whether the patient could wait. I asked Priya to ring the district medical officer and find out. She said she would do it. Then I turned to Tunde and asked him to stand with the patient and watch his pulse and his skin. He stood at the bedside. Then I sat down beside Okafor.

Okafor had been watching the man's leg for twenty minutes. He said, "Put pressure on the wound, not on the pack. She has been pressing on the pack. The pack goes deeper than the cut."

Priya was on the phone. Tunde was watching the monitor. I could see both of them about to argue, and I did not want that argument in front of the man. So I told them to finish their work first, and that we would talk in the morning. Okafor said nothing. He went back to his chair.

I was wrong to send him away. That was the whole of my mistake. I had spent the evening asking everyone what they thought, and then I had not wanted to hear it. BERNIE
That was the most useful thing anyone has said all day.

If you want a short walk with a view, the trail to Mather Point is flat. About a mile.

A mile.

Up and down.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin on any given Thursday and you will probably see bread, a few wilted greens, a carrot that went soft in the drawer, maybe some rice left over from Sunday. In many homes, a large share of the food that gets thrown away follows a familiar path. It is bought, it is forgotten, it goes bad, and then it is tossed. You do not need to change everything at once. You only need to know where the food goes to waste in your own kitchen, and then plan around that.

Start with the shopping list, because that is where the waste actually begins. Most of us shop hungry, and a hungry person buys things they do not need. Eat something before you go, and take a quick look in the fridge and the freezer first. The eggs in the back and the frozen peas are already taken care of. Then plan around what you already have, and write down only what is missing. When you are at the store, be firm about what is on the list and easy about everything else. A loose carrot that is on sale is fine. Two bags of chips that are not on the list are where the waste starts.

Buy loose produce when you can, and leave the pre-packed salad and the four-pack of mushrooms on the shelf if you are not sure you will use them. It is easy to say you will eat something fresh, but what you actually eat is a better guide. The same goes for meat and fish. Freeze what you will not cook within a day or two, and put the earliest items at the front of the freezer so they get eaten first.

Storage is the second thing, and much of it is simple. Keep the fruit and veg where they belong. Potatoes and onions like a cool, dark cupboard. Leafy greens need the cold and some air, so keep them in the fridge and do not seal them in a plastic bag. Herbs last longer with their stems in a glass of water, loosely covered. Bread goes mouldy in a bag on the counter and goes stale in the fridge, so keep it in a bread bin or a paper bag, and freeze what you will not eat in a few days. If bread goes hard, it is still good for toast, croutons and puddings.

Some of this is about air and moisture. Lettuce wilts in a sealed bag and turns slimy in a damp one, so dry it well after washing and keep it loosely wrapped. Berries go mouldy quickly, and they tend to spoil the whole punnet, so pick through them when you get home and freeze the soft ones. Root vegetables keep for weeks in a cool place.

The freezer is your best friend in this, and most of us use it for ice cream and peas. Cooked meat, bread, fruit that has gone soft, blanched greens, stock, even a jar of pesto, will all keep in the freezer for months. Label things with the date, because frozen food keeps forever and nobody can tell from a frozen block of sauce what it is. When you defrost something, do it in the fridge, never on the counter.

Leftovers are the third thing, and they do not have to mean eating the same thing twice. Ask yourself what a leftover is good for before you ask what it is. Last night's roast potatoes are this morning's fried potatoes with onion. Cooked rice that has gone a bit dry makes good fried rice or a pudding. The Wednesday curry becomes Thursday's pasta sauce. Cook once and eat twice on purpose. Make bigger portions of things you freeze well, and freeze half before you sit down to eat.

If you have a compost bin or a council collection, put your peelings, tea bags and eggshells in it. What goes in the bin still costs you something, whether it goes in the trash or the compost.

Scrap use is where people get stuck, so here is a short list. Onion and garlic skins, carrot tops, celery leaves and mushroom stems all make a good vegetable stock when you simmer them and strain it. Freeze the scraps in a bag through the week and make stock on the weekend. Bread that has gone hard is the oldest scrap there is. Croutons, breadcrumbs for topping a casserole, a bread pudding, or French toast for breakfast. Milk that is just past its date will usually still go into a cake, a pancake batter or a cheese sauce, as long as it smells all right. The "use by" date is about safety, and eggs and milk keep a little past it if they smell fine. The "best before" date is about quality, and food is often perfectly good after it. If a date is the only reason something is going in the bin, smell it and look at it first.

One thing is worth saying straight. Some of this costs nothing, like freezing the bread. Some of it costs a freezer bag and a label. Some of it means eating more beans, because a packed lunch of chickpeas and rice costs very little. If you are short of money, that matters more than anything else in this article. Eating the leftovers and freezing the bread will save you money as well as time.

Where to start this week: look in the bin, plan one shopping trip around what you already have, and freeze what you cannot use. That is it. Next week, add one more thing.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review brings together the main findings from the past forty years of research on physical activity and depression. The evidence is large and consistent enough that the relationship is now treated as established. The details are less settled. They differ by the kind of activity, the dose, the severity of the depression, and which outcomes are measured.

What the studies show

Prevention. In prospective studies, people who were physically active had a substantially lower risk of developing depression later, generally about a quarter to a third less, across a wide range of follow-up periods. The effect holds for leisure activity, occupational activity and exercise taken for fitness. Active people also tend to sleep better and report fewer physical symptoms, and both of those are linked to later depression.

Treating existing depression. Meta-analyses of randomised trials, mostly in adults with major depressive disorder, find that exercise produces a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms, with effect sizes usually around half a standard deviation. The effect is seen with aerobic exercise, resistance training and combined programmes, and it appears across different settings: clinics, community programmes and home-based trials. Several large trials have compared exercise with usual care or with antidepressant medication. In mild to moderate depression, exercise was often as effective as medication. In more severe depression, the results are mixed, with some trials finding exercise adds to treatment as much as it stands alone. There is also evidence that people who keep exercising after a course of treatment are less likely to relapse, though the trials here are fewer and the results vary.

Who has been studied. Most of the evidence comes from adults. Trials in adolescents show a smaller and less consistent effect, though the prevention findings in young people are reasonably steady. Older adults, people with long-term physical illness, and postpartum women are less well represented.

Possible mechanisms

The causes are almost certainly several at once, and researchers still argue about how much each one contributes.

Neurotransmitters. Exercise raises levels of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine in brain regions that regulate mood, and these are the same systems that most antidepressant drugs act on. The increase is real but modest, and it is probably part of the picture rather than the whole of it.

Neurotrophic factors. Repeated exercise raises BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells survive and grow. In people with depression, BDNF is often lower than in healthy people. Higher BDNF is linked to better response to treatment. Whether exercise works partly by raising BDNF is well supported in animals and reasonably well supported in people.

Stress hormones. Regular activity tends to lower the body's stress response, with smaller rises in cortisol for a given stressor and better recovery afterward. It also seems to improve how the body handles inflammation, which is often raised in depression.

Other factors. Sleep, circadian rhythm, inflammation, insulin sensitivity and the gut microbiome all move with exercise, and each one is linked to depression. They are plausible contributors, and the evidence for each varies.

Endorphins and endocannabinoids may play a role, but their part is less clearly established.

What seems to work

There is no single dose that fits everyone, and the numbers below are rough. People with depression often begin from a low base, so the first gain usually comes from doing something rather than from doing a lot.

Frequency. Most of the benefit in prevention comes from being active on most days, roughly four to seven days a week. For treatment, trials commonly use three to five sessions a week.

Duration. Short bouts count. Sessions of about thirty minutes on most days are linked to a meaningful reduction in symptoms. Gains appear at around twenty minutes and keep growing with more, at least up to about an hour.

Intensity. Moderate intensity, where a person can talk but not sing, seems to offer most of the benefit. Vigorous effort adds some extra effect in some trials, but also more dropouts. For someone very depressed, moderate is usually the better starting point.

Type. Aerobic exercise, resistance training and mind-body exercise such as yoga and tai chi all produce benefits. Resistance training deserves specific mention for people who are older, frail or recovering from illness. Yoga and tai chi add something of their own: attention to the body, breath and a calming practice, which may matter for people whose depression comes with anxiety or rumination.

Social context. Group exercise and walking with another person add a social element. Social contact is a known factor in recovery, and it may be why some people do better in a class or a walking group.

Matching the dose to the person

Mild depression. Exercise on its own is a reasonable first option, alongside or instead of medication, with the person's preferences deciding. Many people with mild depression find a daily walk they can keep up.

Moderate depression. Exercise as part of a plan, usually alongside therapy and possibly medication.

Severe depression. Exercise as an add-on to standard treatment. Starting is often the hardest part. A short walk some days is a real beginning, and the plan grows from there.

People who cannot exercise much. For someone who can only manage a few minutes a day, the gain is still likely to be there. The aim is to keep doing it.

Challenges and barriers

Starting is hard for the person. Low energy, poor sleep, loss of interest and psychomotor slowing are features of depression, and exercise asks for energy, a routine and effort just when the person has least of each. Early gains are often in sleep and energy, with mood following a few weeks later, so a person who feels nothing after a week may stop.

Adherence. Dropouts in exercise trials are common, especially in the first months, and are often due to the same difficulties that depression brings.

The body weight problem. Depression is linked with weight gain, and some antidepressants cause it. Exercise helps with weight for some people and hardly at all for others. It should not be sold as a weight solution, or people quickly learn that it does not work.

Barriers in clinical care. Time, funding and referral pathways are the main ones. Depression services have little time for exercise, and exercise services have little time for depression. Many clinicians were not trained to prescribe it. Exercise is often left to the patient as general advice, and advice alone produces small changes.

Barriers outside care. Cost, access to safe places, work and care duties, and past bad experiences with sport. For some people, especially women and older adults, gym culture is a real barrier, and home or street-based activity removes it.

Measurement problems. Studies use many different measures of activity, from questionnaires that people with depression may answer more pessimistically to accelerometers. Some trials are small, and the blinding is poor. Nobody can be blinded to whether they have been running.

The relationship runs both ways. Depression reduces activity, and low activity raises the risk of depression, so the line between cause and effect runs in both directions. Much of the prevention evidence is observational, which is why it shows association more firmly than cause.

Where the evidence is thin

The optimal dose for severe depression, and whether more intensity brings more benefit or simply more dropouts, is not settled. The long-term effect on relapse is less firmly established than the short-term effect on symptoms. For children and adolescents, the prevention findings are steadier than the treatment findings. There is also limited research on how to get people to keep exercising once a clinical programme ends.

Takeaway. For most people, a moderate session most days, done in a form they will keep doing, is a reasonable minimum, and more tends to bring more benefit.

"Offcuts and Wonder: Making Better Art with Less"
Your name, context
Visual: one sculpture built entirely from discarded material, lit so the repairs show.

Slide 1. The shelf in the back room
Script: "Look at this shelf. It's in the back room of every studio I've worked in, mine included. It holds the jars we won't use: the blue that came out wrong, the glue that went cloudy, the acrylics that dried in the tubes. Artists are among the worst offenders at throwing away what's still good. We buy fresh for every project, and the old stuff goes in the bin because it's not quite right. Today I want to show you that the offcut is the best material in the studio. It has a story, it costs nothing, and it's already half worked. And the people around you are throwing that away right now."
Visual: a photo of a real shelf, labelled. Leave the next slide blank.

Slide 2. What happens to it
Script: "Where does it go? In many places it goes to landfill, where it breaks down slowly and releases methane as it does. Paint and glue go in the liquid waste. Solvents often go down the drain. One student project's worth of acrylics can pollute more water than a family uses in a month. I'll show you a number on the next slide. It's a rough one, from figures the industry publishes, and I'd rather you took it as an order of magnitude than as a measurement."
Visual: a simple diagram, material in, landfill and drain out. No numbers yet.

Slide 3. The number
Script: "Here's the figure. Making new acrylic paint takes a great deal of water and energy, and the pigment is the most polluting part of the process. One tube of fresh paint does more harm than all the water you could save by washing brushes in a jar and reusing it. I'm fairly sure of the direction. The exact figure depends on how you make the paint, and nobody knows it well. Read it as: it's a lot, and the true number might be more."
Visual: the same diagram with one large number over the tube.

Slide 4. The mended bowl
Script: "This is a bowl a friend of mine made. It cracked. She didn't throw it away. She mended it with gold lacquer, and now the crack is the best part of the bowl. People have mended things with gold for a very long time. The Japanese call it kintsugi. In many places, broken pottery was once collected and recycled into new vessels. The idea is old. So is the shame of having something broken. Gold lacquer is expensive. This is a cheap version. It's also a lesson: a break doesn't end a thing. It becomes its history."
Visual: the bowl, before and after, the crack in gold close up.

Slide 5. The bag that outlasted the coat
Script: "This is a bag I made from an old wool coat. Wool lasts a very long time. The coat was worn out at the collar and the sleeves, and the body was fine. I cut it up and sewed it into a bag. It's held up for years. The people who mend clothes, seamstresses and tailors, knew this for a long time. They patched, they turned things inside out, and they let out hems. A coat that gets mended at forty still has life in it at fifty. Most of us throw away good material because it's out of fashion. This one was out of fashion for a season."
Visual: the coat on a hanger, then the bag, then the bag on a shelf after years of use.

Slide 6. What it costs
Script: "Now the cost, because it isn't free. It costs time. Reusing is slower than buying fresh. On a big job I work out early which offcuts to save and which to use up, because a box of scraps that never gets touched is just clutter. It costs a bit of nerve. Using the blue that came out wrong means accepting that it might come out wrong again. And it costs nothing at all if nobody sees. That's the trade I'd tell you about straight. Here's what you get back. You learn what your materials are like, because you only have one tube and you learn to use it well. You have something to tell people. And the waste never happens, so nobody has to clean it up."
Visual: a scale. On one side, time and nerve. On the other, skill, story and nothing thrown away.

Slide 7. Show and tell
Script: "I've brought some things. There's a jar of paint I mixed from tubes that were nearly dry. There's a piece of board someone else discarded. And there's a small sample of the waste from a class project, so you can see it with your own eyes. Pass it around."
Visual: none. The objects are on a table beside you.
Ask: "How many of you have a jar like this at home?" Let them answer.

Slide 8. Try it now
Script: "Here's what I want you to do today. Take a scrap and make something in five minutes. A badge, a card, a tag. It doesn't have to be good. It has to be yours. And before you start, look around the room. What's already here that someone else threw out?"
Visual: a timer on the screen, set to five minutes.

Slide 9. Who else is affected
Script: "You are not the only person this touches. The person who cleans your studio or the school's workshop handles the waste, and so do their lungs. Then there's everyone downstream of the drain. And further out, the people who live near the places where the raw materials are made. Further out still, the animals and the forests. The person closest to you counts for more with you, and so does the one cleaning up after you. They count for less the further away they are, and they still count. The waste doesn't stay in the studio. It goes somewhere."
Visual: a set of rings, you at the centre, then the studio, then the neighbourhood, then further out.

Slide 10. One small thing
Script: "Choose one thing this week. One jar, one box, one old thing you've been meaning to bin. That's all. A habit you can keep for a year beats a perfect rule you drop in February."
Visual: one jar on a shelf, lit.

Slide 11. Call to action
Script: "Here's what I'd ask. This week, keep one jar. At the end of the month, bring one object made from something you found or someone else threw away, and show it to a friend. And one question for your next project: what's already here? If you take one thing from today, make it that. The best material is the one already in your room."
Visual: the three steps as three icons. A question mark over the last one.

Slide 12. Questions
Visual: the shelf from slide 1, back again.
Script: "Questions. And if you have a jar at home, I'd love to hear about it."

How to keep them engaged

Keep the first reveal blank. People lean in when they can't see the answer yet. Show the shelf photo first and let them guess what's on it. Then show the real shelf, and a few will laugh at their own boxes.

Let them touch it. The object in your hand counts for more than a slide. The jar of mixed paint is the strongest prop you have, because it looks a bit odd and someone will ask how it works.

Give them five minutes. A small task done in the room turns them from listeners into makers. The badge is theirs by the end of the talk.

Ask, then tell. On the costs slide, ask them first what they'd lose by reusing. They'll say "it takes longer" before you do. When they say it themselves, they're less likely to argue with it.

End on a question. A talk that ends with what's already here lingers longer than one that ends with landfill.

Be honest about the limits. Saying "it takes nerve" makes the rest more believable. An audience catches a hidden cost quickly, and once they catch one, they stop trusting the rest of the talk.

If you want a handout, one page is enough. Three steps, the order of magnitude figure with its source, and a sketch of the bowl before and after. People take home what's on paper.

If you tell me who they are, students, a makerspace or a school, I can change the examples. A primary class needs a different slide 8 from a group of professional designers.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well after sixty is mostly about keeping the habits you already have and changing the ones that no longer serve you. This guide will help you plan your meals, shop for them, keep them safe, and eat them at times that suit your body.

Before you begin, if you have a doctor or a dietitian who knows your health, ask them to look at what you eat. They know things about your body that no general guide can.

How much you need

As you age, you usually need fewer calories because you move less and your body uses energy differently. But you still need the same amount, or even more, of certain nutrients. You need protein at every meal to keep your muscles strong. You need calcium and vitamin D for your bones. You need iron, vitamin B12, and folate for your blood. If you have lost weight without trying, or if you are eating much less than you used to, tell your doctor. That is worth finding out sooner rather than later.

Portions

You do not need to count anything. Use your hands. A serving of protein is about the size of your palm. A serving of starch, such as potatoes, rice or bread, is about the size of your closed fist. Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit. Fill the other half with protein and starch. Drink water or unsweetened tea most of the time. If you are on a liquid diet or have trouble swallowing, ask your doctor or a speech therapist how to eat and drink safely.

Meal preparation

Keep it simple. Cook in batches on a day when you have energy, such as Saturday, and freeze portions you will not eat that week. Soft foods are easy to chew and easy to digest. Stew, soup, slow-cooker or steamed meals are good choices. Cut food into small pieces. If you cook for one, frozen vegetables and pre-cooked grains such as quinoa or couscous save time and do not go bad.

Cost

Plan around what is on sale. Buy frozen fruit and vegetables. They are picked at their ripest and frozen, so they often have more nutrients than produce that has travelled far. Canned beans, lentils and tuna are cheap, last a long time, and need no refrigeration. Eggs are one of the cheapest sources of protein. Buy store brand. You pay less and get the same food.

Foods to limit

Most seniors should eat less salt, less saturated fat and less added sugar. Read the labels. Low sodium means less salt. Low fat means less saturated fat. Low sugar means less added sugar. The sugar in fruit is fine. The sugar in a sweet drink is the kind you want to avoid.

Diabetes

Keep to your doctor's plan for blood sugar, meals and medication. Eat at regular times. Do not skip meals. Carbohydrates raise your blood sugar, so eat them at the same times each day and in the same amounts. Choose whole grains, beans, lentils, vegetables and fruit. Limit white bread, white rice, sweet drinks and sweets. Check your blood sugar as your doctor has told you. If you use insulin or tablets that lower your blood sugar, ask your doctor what to eat when you are too unwell to eat normally.

High blood pressure

Limit salt. A small amount can make a large difference. Do not add salt at the table. Use herbs, garlic, lemon and pepper instead. Eat potassium-rich foods such as bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes and leafy greens, unless your doctor has told you to limit them, for example if you have kidney disease. Check with your doctor before you use a salt substitute. Many of them contain potassium.

Heart disease

Eat less saturated fat. That means less fatty meat, less full-fat dairy and less coconut oil. Choose fish and oily fish such as salmon and mackerel twice a week. Choose poultry, eggs, beans and lentils for most other protein. Eat nuts and seeds without salt. Do not eat trans fat. That means less margarine and fewer packaged pastries.

The plan below is a sample. Swap in foods you like and leave out anything you cannot eat.

Day one. Breakfast: oatmeal made with water or milk, a sliced banana and a spoon of ground flaxseed. Lunch: tuna and bean salad with cucumber, tomato and a little olive oil and lemon. Dinner: chicken and vegetable soup, a slice of wholegrain bread, and a piece of fruit. Snack: yoghurt or a boiled egg.

Day two. Breakfast: two scrambled eggs, spinach and tomato, and a slice of wholegrain toast. Lunch: leftover chicken soup and a piece of fruit. Dinner: baked fish, mashed potato and steamed broccoli. Snack: apple slices with a little peanut butter.

Day three. Breakfast: porridge made with milk, grated apple and cinnamon. Lunch: wholegrain wrap with hummus, cucumber and shredded carrot. Dinner: lentil stew or a bean and vegetable curry with rice. Snack: a piece of fruit and a few unsalted nuts.

Storage

Label everything you freeze with the date. Use frozen meals within three months. Thaw in the fridge, never on the bench. Reheat until it is steaming hot all the way through, and eat it the same day. Do not reheat the same leftovers twice. Keep your fridge at or below four degrees.

Food safety

Wash your hands before you handle food. Wash fruit and vegetables under running water, even those you will peel. Keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food. Do not taste food to decide whether it has gone bad. If it smells strange, looks strange or has been left out too long, throw it away. When you are unsure, throw it out.

Meal timings

Eat breakfast within an hour or two of waking. It breaks the fast and gives you the energy to get through the morning. Have your largest meal at midday or early evening, not late at night. A heavy dinner late in the evening can sit badly with some conditions, such as reflux, and can make sleep worse. Eat something small if you go more than four or five hours between meals and you are on a medication that needs food. Many people who take tablets for diabetes or blood thinners are in this group. Ask your doctor. Drink most of your fluids earlier in the day. If you wake at night to pass water, drink less in the hour or two before bed, but do not drink less overall.

Other things that affect what you eat

If you eat alone, eating with someone else, even a neighbour or a staff member at a day centre, usually means a better meal. If you have trouble seeing, label the fridge and the cupboard with large print or with bright stickers. If you have trouble standing for long periods, sit while you prepare food. If you have trouble with stairs, keep your snacks on the floor where you live so you do not have to climb for them. If you are on a fixed income, ask your doctor or a social worker about food support, a pensioner's concession card or local food programs. Many places have them, and people use them more than they expect.

If you tell me what you have at home now, what you enjoy, and whether you cook for one or for a family, I can draw up a plan for the whole week.
