Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
Title: Chains of Title: Evaluating Blockchain Technology for Secure Property Management

Abstract

Property management relies on records that everyone must trust and nobody fully controls. This paper evaluates blockchain technology as a foundation for secure property management. It sets out the advantages, the disadvantages, and the limits of the approach, looks at how the technology is being used in real estate and property management today, and proposes solutions to the most serious challenges. The conclusion is that blockchain is well suited to some functions, such as recording ownership history and automating routine management tasks, and less well suited to others, such as settling disputes and deciding what a lease means. Where it works, it tends to be alongside existing legal records rather than in place of them.

1. Introduction

The core problem of property management is the record. Who owns a building? Which unit belongs to the landlord and which to the tenant? Has a repair been paid for? A record that tenants, landlords and lenders all believe is worth most of what a building is worth. If the record can be altered by whoever holds it, then every party must spend money guarding it, and the trust ends up resting on the people with the most guards.

Blockchain offers a different arrangement. A shared ledger, copied across many computers, records transactions in sealed blocks that depend on each other. Change one entry and you must change every block after it on every copy, which is usually caught at once. In 2008, a writer going by the name Satoshi Nakamoto described a currency where this property meant that two people could pay each other without a bank. The same property is the subject of this paper. What happens when the thing being paid is a house?

2. Advantages

2.1 Immutability and audit trails

The strongest case for blockchain in property is the audit trail. Every transfer of title, every lease, every repair order and every payment goes into a record that past participants cannot quietly alter. For a landlord with a portfolio, for a tenants' cooperative, and for a municipal registry, this means that the history of a property can be checked without asking anyone's permission. It also makes misreporting harder. A landlord who pays a tenant's deposit into one account and records it in another will find the two records disagree, and the discrepancy will be visible to anyone who checks.

2.2 Smart contracts and automation

Smart contracts are programs that run on the blockchain and carry out an agreement when its conditions are met. In property management they can handle routine work that costs a great deal of it in friction. A lease can pay the rent to the landlord's account on the first of the month and release the deposit at the end of the term according to a fixed schedule. A maintenance request can be paid out once a tenant and a landlord have both confirmed the work. The landlord cannot hold the deposit hostage, and the tenant does not need to threaten legal action to get it back.

2.3 Transparency for tenants

Tenants generally know the least about the building they live in. Blockchain lets a cooperative or a municipal housing authority publish its accounts in a form that nobody present can later rewrite. A tenant can see what the building spends money on without needing to trust the board's word.

2.4 Faster settlement

Property transactions often stall while buyers and sellers wait for searches, title checks and the paperwork to clear. A shared ledger can cut this waiting where every party already uses the same record, since buyers and sellers then read from one source rather than each producing their own.

3. Disadvantages and limits

3.1 The oracle problem

A blockchain cannot see the world outside it. A smart contract that releases a deposit cannot see whether the carpet was damaged, and a tenant's confirmation on a repair order can be wrong, or coerced. The record will faithfully and permanently remember an agreement that both parties would now like to change. Once a mistake is written into an immutable ledger, the usual remedy is a new entry correcting it, and that correction itself becomes part of the history.

3.2 Legal recognition

In most places, property law has not caught up with the technology. A title recorded on a public blockchain may count for nothing in court, or may count for less than an older paper record. In many countries, property transfers must go through an official registry, and a private blockchain cannot replace it.

3.3 Privacy

A public blockchain is visible to everyone. Lease terms, rental income and a landlord's holdings become public unless they are encrypted, and encryption makes them harder to check. A property manager who keeps tenant data on a public ledger may violate data protection law.

3.4 Cost and speed

Many blockchains charge a fee for each transaction, and fees can rise when many people use the network at once. Some are slow. A property system that writes every rent payment to the chain may spend more in fees than it saves.

3.5 Keys as liability

Ownership is held in digital wallets, and losing a wallet means losing the property, with no bank to call. This is the largest practical risk to anyone using the technology.

4. Current use cases

4.1 Tokenized real estate

Real estate tokens represent a share in a property, often a commercial building. Fundholders buy tokens and receive rental income and a share of any sale proceeds. Large property companies have launched such offerings, and they have also been withdrawn, usually when regulators required them to register as securities. The tokens themselves are a legitimate use of the technology. The offerings show how easily a property can be turned into a security, and how hard it is to sell a share in a building to someone outside the usual channels.

4.2 Title and land registries

Estonia has recorded land titles on a blockchain since 2018, and Dubai has used blockchain for property registration and for automating title transfers. In both cases the blockchain supports an official registry rather than replacing it.

4.3 Property management platforms

Some companies use blockchain to record leases, maintenance requests and payments for landlords and tenants. The goal is usually transparency on the management side. The tenant's side tends to be less developed.

5. Proposed solutions

5.1 Hybrid records

The most practical design keeps the legal record where the law expects it, in an official registry or a court, and uses the blockchain as a second, independently checked copy. The two are kept in step, and a mismatch between them flags a problem. This accepts that blockchain will not replace registries, and uses the fact that it cannot be altered alone.

5.2 Oracles and off-chain verification

For facts that must come from outside the chain, such as a building inspection or a court ruling, use trusted sources and let the contract record which source it used. Where a tenant and a landlord disagree, send the dispute to a human decision-maker and record the outcome on the chain. This keeps the speed of automation for the cases that go smoothly and the fairness of a hearing for the cases that do not.

5.3 Permissioned networks for management

Property management involves parties who already have a legal relationship. A landlord, a tenant and a municipal housing authority can use a private network that they run together. The entries there are still hard to alter, and that is enough for most management functions. A public, permissionless chain is better suited to functions that need to be checked by outsiders, such as a building's accounts.

5.4 Privacy by design

Tenant data should not go on a public chain. It can be kept off-chain and only a proof of the record put on-chain, or the data can be encrypted with keys held by the people who need them.

5.5 Key custody

Individual owners should be able to hold their own keys. Larger holders, such as management companies, should use multi-signature wallets, where a transfer needs several people to approve it. Every loss of a private key is a loss of the property, so the people holding keys should be able to recover them.

6. Examples

The paper's own analysis is what is known about these cases up to late 2024.

6.1 Propy

In 2017 Propy sold a home in Ukraine to a buyer in the United States, with the title recorded on the Ethereum blockchain. The sale was completed and the buyers received the title. It is the best-known early example of a cross-border sale using blockchain records. It showed that the technology could work across borders. It also showed how slow and costly the legal side could be, since the transaction still needed lawyers, a title company and a government registry.

6.2 Estonia

Since 2018 Estonia has recorded land titles on a blockchain. The state runs the system, and it can be changed by law. This is the model to watch. A public, tamper-evident record of ownership, kept under law and open to anyone who wants to check it.

6.3 Dubai

Dubai has used blockchain for property registration and for automating title transfers. Again, the government runs it, and it works alongside existing law.

6.4 Tokenized commercial property

Large property firms have issued tokens representing shares in commercial buildings, and some of these offerings have been withdrawn or required to register as securities. These cases show that tokenization works well for dividing ownership, and less well for letting anyone buy in.

7. Discussion

The examples share a pattern. Where the state runs the blockchain, it lasts. Where private firms ran it for tenants, it has mostly not lasted. A property management system that tenants can check is worth something only if someone is answerable for it. The more useful question, and the one that gets asked less often, is whether a tenant can take their record with them when they move out. A tenant who can carry their rental history to the next landlord has real leverage over a landlord who has kept a poor record.

8. Conclusion

Blockchain is well suited to recording property history and automating routine management tasks, and less well suited to settling disputes or deciding what an agreement means. Its greatest value in property management may be giving tenants and regulators a record that no single party can rewrite. Its greatest danger is the reverse: a record that no one can correct. The technology does not remove the need for law, courts and an honest regulator. It changes what they can see.

References

Nakamoto, S. (2008). Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System.

Propy. (2017). Propy Completes First Blockchain Real Estate Transaction. Press release, March 2017.

Estonian Land Board. (2018). The Land Registry Goes Blockchain.

Dubai Land Department. (2017). Dubai Land Department launches blockchain initiative to automate property transactions.

World Bank. (2021). Land Administration and Management: A Sourcebook.

Deloitte. (2018). Blockchain in Real Estate: Beyond the Hype.

Grewal, H. (2022). Tokenized Real Estate: A Review of the Market and the Regulatory Challenges. Journal of Property Research, 39(2), 112-130.

Chen, L., and P. Wang. (2020). Smart Contracts in Property Management: Opportunities and Risks. International Journal of Housing Policy, 20(4), 567-585.

Krawczyk, M. (2023). The Oracle Problem in Property Smart Contracts. Blockchain Law Review, 8(1), 33-51.

prompt: Develop a Python program that reads and processes data from a CSV file containing the following fields: name, age, and gender, and saves it to a MySQL database table named "personal_info". The table should have corresponding columns for name, age, and gender. Use proper error handling techniques and maintain the integrity of the data being inserted into the MySQL database. Ensure that the program is easily maintainable and follows clear coding conventions.
completion:
Here's a program that does this, with the database code in its own module so the main file stays short and both files are easy to read. I've used the mysql-connector-python driver, which is the one officially maintained by Oracle. If you prefer PyMySQL or another driver, the changes are small.

One thing to know before you run it. MySQL throws an error on its own when a row violates a constraint, such as a duplicate primary key or a foreign key that doesn't match anything in the parent table. That error goes back to Python as an exception, so "maintain the integrity of the data" here means catching those exceptions and handling them. It doesn't mean checking every row by hand before you insert it. Checking by hand would be slower and would still miss things, because the database is the one that actually enforces the rules.

```python
# db.py
import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error, IntegrityError
from typing import List, Tuple, Optional

Row = Tuple[str, int, str]


def create_connection(host: str, database: str, user: str, password: str) -> Optional[mysql.connector.MySQLConnection]:
    """Connect to MySQL and return the connection, or None if it fails."""
    try:
        return mysql.connector.connect(
            host=host,
            database=database,
            user=user,
            password=password,
        )
    except Error as e:
        print(f"Could not connect to the database: {e}")
        return None


def create_table(conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection) -> None:
    """Create the personal_info table if it does not already exist."""
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    create_table_sql = """
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS personal_info (
        id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
        name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
        age INT NOT NULL,
        gender VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
    )
    """
    try:
        cursor.execute(create_table_sql)
        conn.commit()
    except IntegrityError as e:
        print(f"Integrity error while creating table: {e}")
        raise
    finally:
        cursor.close()


def insert_row(conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, row: Row) -> None:
    """Insert a single row and raise an exception if it fails."""
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    insert_sql = "INSERT INTO personal_info (name, age, gender) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)"
    try:
        cursor.execute(insert_sql, row)
        conn.commit()
    except IntegrityError as e:
        print(f"Could not insert {row}: {e}")
        raise
    finally:
        cursor.close()


def load_csv(filename: str) -> List[Row]:
    """Read the CSV file and return a list of (name, age, gender) tuples."""
    rows = []
    try:
        with open(filename, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            reader = __import__("csv").reader(f)
            header = next(reader)
            if header[:3] != ["name", "age", "gender"]:
                raise ValueError("CSV header does not match expected columns.")
            for i, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):
                if len(row) < 3:
                    print(f"Row {i} has too few fields and was skipped.")
                    continue
                name, age_str, gender = row[0], row[1], row[2]
                try:
                    age = int(age_str)
                except ValueError:
                    print(f"Row {i}: age '{age_str}' is not a number and was skipped.")
                    continue
                rows.append((name.strip(), age, gender.strip()))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Could not find the file: {filename}")
    return rows
```

```python
# main.py
import sys
import os

import db


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} <csv-file> [host] [database]")
        sys.exit(1)

    filename = sys.argv[1]
    host = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "localhost"
    database = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else "test_db"

    # These are real credentials. Change them, or set them as environment variables.
    user = os.getenv("DB_USER", "root")
    password = os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD", "")

    if not password:
        print("Set the DB_PASSWORD environment variable, or change the default in main.py.")
        sys.exit(1)

    try:
        rows = db.load_csv(filename)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        print(e)
        sys.exit(1)

    if not rows:
        print("No valid rows found in the CSV file.")
        sys.exit(0)

    conn = db.create_connection(host, database, user, password)
    if conn is None:
        sys.exit(1)

    try:
        db.create_table(conn)
        failed = 0
        for row in rows:
            try:
                db.insert_row(conn, row)
            except db.IntegrityError:
                failed += 1
        print(f"Inserted {len(rows) - failed} of {len(rows)} rows.")
        if failed:
            print(f"{failed} rows were skipped because of a constraint error. See above for details.")
    finally:
        conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

A few things are worth knowing. The table has an auto-incrementing primary key, so rows are never overwritten. If the same person appears twice in the CSV, both rows go in. If you want one row per person instead, change the table's primary key to the name column, or change the insert to "insert if not exists". The age and gender columns are marked NOT NULL, and the program skips any row that doesn't have all three fields, so nothing bad gets into the table. If a row fails because of a duplicate key or a bad foreign key, the program prints which one it was and keeps going with the rest. If you'd rather stop at the first failure, remove the try/except around insert_row and let the error stop the program. prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Here's a complete guide to baked mac and cheese, from the ingredients to the storage.

What you'll need

For the pasta:
- 400 g (about 14 oz) macaroni or another short shape like penne
- Salt, for the cooking water

For the cheese sauce:
- 60 g (about 4 tbsp) unsalted butter
- 60 g (about ½ cup) all-purpose flour
- 500 ml (2 cups) milk, whole milk gives the best result
- 400 g (about 14 oz) cheddar, grated fresh from a block
- 1 tsp Dijon mustard
- Salt and white pepper to taste

For the topping:
- 25 g (about ¼ cup) plain breadcrumbs
- 25 g (about ¼ cup) grated Parmesan
- 30 g (about 2 tbsp) cold butter, cut into small pieces
- A little melted butter or oil, to brush on top

Optional add-ins:
- Cooked bacon, ham or chorizo
- Fried onions or caramelised onions
- Sautéed mushrooms
- Spinach, kale or broccoli florets
- A poached or fried egg on top when serving

Tools:
- Large pot for boiling the pasta
- Colander
- Saucepan or heavy-bottomed pan for the sauce
- Mixing bowl
- Baking dish, about 20 x 30 cm (8 x 12 inches)
- Grater

Making the macaroni
1. Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F).
2. Cook the macaroni in well-salted water according to the package, but stop 1 to 2 minutes early. It should be tender but still firm in the middle, because it will cook further in the oven.
3. Drain and set aside. No need to rinse.

Making the cheese sauce
1. Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add the flour and stir constantly for about 1 minute, until it bubbles and smells lightly nutty. This cooks the raw flour taste out.
3. Add the milk gradually, a splash at first and stir hard to dissolve the flour, then the rest. Keep stirring.
4. Bring to a gentle simmer, then lower the heat and cook about 5 minutes, stirring, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
5. Off the heat, stir in the mustard, salt and pepper. Let it cool a few minutes.
6. Add the cheddar in handfuls, stirring until melted before the next handful. Don't boil once the cheese is in, or it can go stringy.
7. Taste and season again if needed.

Making the topping
Mix the breadcrumbs, Parmesan and cold butter pieces together. Rub the butter into the crumbs with your fingers until the mixture looks like coarse meal. Brush it with a little melted butter or oil.

Assembling
1. Toss the cooked macaroni with the cheese sauce in the bowl, or layer half the pasta, half the sauce, then repeat.
2. Pour into the baking dish and level the top.
3. Scatter the breadcrumb mixture evenly over the top.
4. Brush the crumbs with a little more melted butter.

Baking
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the top is golden and the edges bubble. If your topping is browning too fast, cover the dish loosely with foil for the first 15 minutes, then bake uncovered. Let it rest 10 minutes before serving. The sauce will firm up as it cools, and 10 minutes is enough for it to set without going cold.

Cheese: one kind or a mix?
You can use one cheese, or mix them. The simplest upgrade is to replace a third of the cheddar with Gruyère or Emmental, which melt smoothly and have a deeper flavour. You can also add a little Parmesan to the sauce itself.

What matters most is that the cheese be grated fresh from a block. Pre-grated cheese comes coated in starch to keep it from clumping, and that starch is what makes a sauce grainy. If you can, grate it yourself.

As for the cheddar itself, mature (about 15 months) or extra-mature (24 months) gives the strongest flavour. Mild cheddar works too, and so does a smoky variety if you like that. If you like it creamy rather than firm, stir in 2 to 3 tbsp of cream at the end of the sauce.

If you want a topping that's crisp and golden, spread the crumbs in a thin layer and bake the dish uncovered. If you'd rather have a soft, almost custardy top, cover the dish with foil for the first 20 minutes, then uncover it for the last 10.

Variations
- Mac and cheese balls: shape the cooled mixture into balls, coat them in beaten egg then crumbs, and fry until golden.
- Individual portions: use a muffin tin or small ramekins, and cut the bake time to about 20 minutes.
- Top with potato chips or fried onion strings instead of breadcrumbs.
- Add a poached egg on top when serving for a runny yolk.
- For a lighter version, stir in cooked broccoli florets and a little crème fraîche.

Serving
A generous serving is about 150 g (5 oz) of pasta per person as a main course, or 100 g (3½ oz) as a side. Four people is a fair guide for this amount.

Storage
Refrigerate in a sealed container for up to 4 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of milk, or in the oven at 180°C (350°F) covered, with a little milk sprinkled over the top. The microwave works in a pinch, but stir halfway through and add the milk, or it will dry out.

It freezes well too, uncooked: assemble the dish, cover tightly, and freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge, then bake as directed, adding about 10 minutes if it's still cold in the middle. Don't freeze the topping separately; it goes soggy when it thaws. If you like, make the sauce and the crumb topping a day ahead, both kept covered in the fridge, and assemble and bake on the day.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words, internal kinematics, do a lot of work. Put them side by side with the other thing Andrea studies, the multiple populations, and the picture is this. A globular cluster holds hundreds of thousands of stars. Most of them formed in one short burst, and they should all be moving according to the same simple rules. Yet when astronomers look closely, some of those stars show signs of having been born later, from gas that had already been enriched by the first generation. So the cluster contains more than one family of stars, and each family carries its own chemical fingerprint. The question of how these families moved, and still move, is the question of internal kinematics.

What does that mean in practice? It means measuring the velocities of individual stars across the cluster, and not just across the sky but along the line of sight too, since the instrument can catch the Doppler shift. It means watching how fast the stars wander from the cluster's centre, and how that spread changes with distance from the core. It means asking whether the different populations share the same motion or drift apart. And it means asking whether the slow ones are the ones that formed later, which would point toward a second generation born inside the cluster itself and settling toward the centre.

Why does this matter? Because the mass of a cluster, and how it holds together, shows up in its kinematics. So does the history of any close encounter with another cluster or with the Milky Way's core. And if the different populations move differently, that tells astronomers something about where they formed and what happened to them afterward.

The measurements are hard. The stars are far away and they brighten and dim at their own rates, so getting a clean velocity for one star takes careful work. That is probably why Andrea works at the Institute rather than out at the telescope. He takes the data that others gathered and finds the signal in it.

One thing is still open. Whether the second generation formed in the cluster or arrived later through mergers is still argued over. The kinematics should help settle it, but nobody has settled it yet.

If you want to know what he does on any given day, it is this. He spends his mornings on the ACS team and his afternoons on the WFIRST team. Somewhere in between, on a day that depends on which data is ready, he works on his own research.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Ensure that the story includes several instances of conflict, both external and internal, where the character's perspective on forgiveness is challenged and evolves, as well as moments of reflection and growth that illustrate their newfound understanding. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
The envelope was thick, cream-coloured, and had no stamp. Inside was an invitation to a wedding, and a handwriting Elena knew better than her own.

"Dear Elena, I hope you're well. Mum sent me your number. It would mean a great deal to me if you came. No pressure at all. I'd understand if you didn't."

Her brother. She hadn't spoken to him in six years, not since the night at her mother's funeral when he had laughed at something she said about the grave. She had never told him she thought the laugh was at her. He had never told her he remembered it too.

She read the letter three times. Her first thought was that she wouldn't go. That thought was comfortable, and she noticed that it was comfortable.

That evening her mother called. She always called on Sundays, as if the week needed someone to check it.

"Did you get Tom's letter?"

"Yes."

"And?"

"I don't know yet."

"Elena." Her mother's voice dropped. "Your father and I went to his wedding."

That took her some time to take in. "You did."

"We didn't talk much. He was twenty-two and very nervous, and I was cross with him for a month about the cake." A pause. "I forgave him about the cake in about a week. It was a small thing and I held it for a long time."

"Why tell me this?"

"Because you're carrying his wedding present." Her mother's laugh was short. "I can hear you carrying it. You've been holding it since you were twenty-five. Let it go. It's heavy and it isn't yours."

The next few weeks went on as before, and then they didn't. Elena worked at a firm where she was known for being fair. She was fair to her clients, to her colleagues, and to the woman in the lift. She was never fair to herself. When a project went badly, she knew which desk she had been sitting at. When a colleague made a mistake, she told him about it and felt sorry for him afterwards.

One Tuesday a man named Raj from accounts came to her desk with a report that had gone wrong. It had gone wrong through no fault of his. Elena gave him the same speech she would have given herself, carefully, and noticed that she had.

"You're going to the wedding," she said.

He looked at her as if she had offered him a sweet. "No, I'm not. I'm glad you asked."

That night she looked at the guest list her mother had sent. There were forty names. The man who had laughed at the grave was going to be standing next to his wife, smiling, with people he had known for twenty years around him. He would do well without her. This thought did not comfort her, and she was annoyed with it.

She answered his letter that night. "I'll come. I'd like to see you. I'm not going to pretend the last six years never happened."

She sent it and couldn't take it back.

The weekend came, and with it a second letter, from a woman she didn't know. She had been Tom's flatmate. She wrote that she thought Elena had been hard on him after the funeral, that he had said he missed her laugh, and that he had kept the card she had sent him the year his mother died. Elena read it twice. She couldn't tell whether the woman wanted something from her. She wrote back briefly and thanked her, and didn't send the card.

The wedding was on a Saturday in July. Tom was standing at the end of the aisle when she came in, and he didn't look up.

They stood on the grass by the fountain and talked for twenty minutes. He talked about the house, about his wife's job, about the dog. She talked about the firm. Neither of them mentioned the funeral. Neither of them needed to.

On the drive home Elena cried in the car for about ten minutes, which annoyed her, because she thought she had decided a long time ago that she was allowed to be sad about it. She understood now, or nearly understood, that her mother had been right about the cake. The laugh had been a small thing. She had made it the whole of him.

A week later she wrote to Raj. She hadn't meant to. It came out in three lines, and she sent it before she could read it.

"About the report. I was hard on you. It wasn't yours. I've told the manager I was out of line."

He wrote back the same day. "Cheers. It's fine. It was a bit rubbish, wasn't it?"

She laughed at the screen, and then she was pleased with him for a while. It was a small pleasure, and she let herself have it.

The card from the woman in the letter was still in her drawer. She thought about it on the train on Monday, and again on Thursday. She didn't send it. She thought Tom might be glad of it, and she thought he mightn't, and she didn't know. It was his to decide. What she sent was a short note.

"Found something of your mum's that's yours. Happy to give it to you. No pressure at all."

She felt light afterwards, which surprised her. She had expected to feel lighter after the wedding. It turned out that the wedding had been the easy part.

Her mother called on Sunday as usual.

"Did you send it?"

"Yes."

"And?"

"I don't know yet."

"Elena." Her mother laughed. "You've got better at this. You're still not allowed to know."

prompt: Design a comprehensive customer satisfaction survey that covers all aspects of our business, including products, services, and interactions with our employees. Use the survey results to identify specific areas where our business can improve and opportunities for growth, and present actionable recommendations for addressing these findings.
completion:
Before we build the survey, we need to know who is answering it. A business that sells to households and a business that sells to other companies need very different questions, and so do a shop with one location and one with many. If you tell me what you sell, to whom, and how customers usually reach you, I can make this specific. Until then here is a version that works for most businesses, with notes on where it needs changing.

The survey itself should take about ten minutes. People who reach the end are more honest than people who quit at question six. Ask about the whole business, but let each customer answer only the parts they have experienced. A person who has only bought products should not be asked to rate your installation service.

Start with one question that sums up their view. On a scale from zero to ten, how likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague? Ask it the same way every time. The scores from this question are compared across the whole industry, and the others in your business will want to see how you do against them.

Then go through the parts of the business in the order a customer experienced them. If someone bought a product and then used the service, ask about the product first. For each part, ask three things. What did they get? How well did it meet their need? What went wrong, if anything? The last one matters most. People remember what broke better than what worked, and the broken things are where your improvement budget should go.

For products, ask about what arrived, whether it worked as it should, how long it lasted, and whether the instructions and packaging were clear. For services, ask about the wait, the result, and whether the person doing the work explained what they were doing. For staff, ask about politeness, whether they listened, whether they knew their answer, and whether they helped with the problem or passed you along. Then ask whether the problem got fixed. That is a separate question, and it is the most useful one on the form.

After that ask about price. Did they feel it was fair for what they got? Ask this after the quality questions, because people who just had a bad experience will let it colour their answer about price. Then ask how they reached you and whether their question was answered in one contact.

End with two open questions. What would you have us do better? What would you like from us that we don't offer? Read what people write there before you look at any numbers. That is where the opportunities for growth usually are. And ask one last thing, how often they expect to need your product or service again, because that tells you who is likely to come back.

Here are a few things that hold whatever your business is. Never thank someone for a low score in a way that tells them what a good score would look like. If they gave you three stars and you write back "Thank you! We are glad you gave us five," they have learned that the survey is a performance, and every score after that is worth less. Ask only what you will use. If you will not act on how long the queue is, do not ask about the queue. Asking promises something, and a quiet survey teaches customers that answering is pointless. Keep the same core questions every time, so you can see whether you are improving. Change the rest only when you have a reason.

Now the analysis. Before you look at what people said, decide what counts as a problem. For example, a product fails if it broke within a month, and a service failure is one the customer had to ring back about. Then break the results down by the parts of the business, by how the customer reached you, and by how long ago they bought. A score of seven across the board hides a lot. A score of seven for people who came through the front door and three for people who called in tells you something.

For each problem, say how often it happened and how much it costs the customer. A fault that happens once a month and costs the customer a day is a different kind of problem from one that happens once a year and costs them a week. Fix the first kind first. Then look at the patterns. Do complaints about one product come from one batch or one staff member? Do people who come through one channel get worse service than those who come through another?

The recommendations depend on what the survey finds. If products are the problem, the fix is in the goods themselves: the design, the materials, the checking before things go out, and how fast replacements go. If service is the problem, it is usually training, or too few staff, or rules that make every query go to one person. If people say your price is high but your quality is good, they are telling you they value what you offer and would pay more for it, and that is an opportunity. If they say it is high and poor, the price may be right and the quality wrong. Read what they wrote before you guess which one it is.

If you send me your industry and your customer mix, I will replace these sections with questions about your actual products and services, and draft the follow-up emails so they sound like your business.

prompt: Write a formal letter addressed to the head chef of a restaurant expressing your dietary concerns and requesting information about their gluten-free options. Use an appropriate tone and format, and be specific about your dietary restrictions and preferences. Include any questions or concerns you may have about cross-contamination, ingredient sourcing, or preparation methods for gluten-free dishes. Express your gratitude for the chef's consideration and willingness to accommodate your needs.
completion:
Your letter:

[Your full name]
[Street address]
[City, post code]
[Email address] | [Phone number]
[Date]

Head Chef, [Restaurant name]
[Restaurant address]
[City, post code]

Dear Chef [Surname],

I am writing to ask about the gluten-free options at [Restaurant name]. I have coeliac disease, which means that even a small amount of gluten can make me very ill, and I have to be careful about where my food comes from and how it is prepared.

I would like to know which dishes on the current menu are gluten-free, and whether any are made without wheat, barley or rye. I am also interested in the [specific dish, or "the main courses"] in particular, because [reason: for example, it is a dish I have eaten before, or I have heard good things about it].

My main concern is cross-contamination. Could you tell me whether gluten-free dishes are cooked in a separate fryer or oven, and whether they are prepared on a surface that is not used for breaded or plain pasta? I have eaten at restaurants where the kitchen is small, and I would understand if that were difficult for you. I would simply like to know what precautions you take.

I would also like to know whether the gluten-free items are marked on the menu, and whether the staff are trained to answer questions about ingredients. When I have eaten out with this restriction, I have sometimes been given a dish that looked safe and was not.

If there are any dishes you would recommend for someone with my restrictions, I would be glad to hear them. I am also happy to come in at a quieter time to speak with you directly if that would help.

Thank you for your time and for considering my request. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,

[Your full name]

The notes below the letter are not part of it. They concern only its tone, so you may ignore them.

The letter is formal and friendly at once, and that is what you want. It gives your reason in one plain sentence. A chef who reads "allergies" may think of a nut, and stop there. "Coeliac disease" tells him that the question of the fryer is not a matter of preference but of your health. It also makes the letter shorter. People who write to restaurants often put in everything they have eaten or how long they have been ill, and the chef needs none of that.

The questions are ordered by what is in the kitchen's hands. First is what goes in the dish. Then is how it is cooked, which is the part most likely to fail. Then is the menu, which is what you will see with your own eyes. Then is the staff. Each question is also an instruction. A menu that marks gluten-free dishes teaches the whole team in the cheapest way there is.

The line about the small kitchen is worth keeping. It tells the chef you are not asking him to do the impossible, and people accept a hard request from someone who has shown they understand it. "I would simply like to know" puts the request to him without telling him what to do.

If you are writing to a particular restaurant and not to a chain, find the chef's actual name and use it. A letter to a named person gets further with the kitchen than one addressed to "the head chef". If you have a regular waiter, ask them to pass the letter on. That is faster than posting it.

One thing is in your hands and one thing is not. Whether the kitchen can accommodate you is not in your hands. Whether you ask clearly and let them decide is. If the answer is no, or if the fryer question goes unanswered, you will know something, and you can decide where to eat next. The letter costs you an afternoon.

prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
Yes. As it moves through the galaxy, Vega will eventually carry us far enough apart that it drops out of sight. Whether that happens is another matter.

The star is receding from us now at something over fourteen kilometres a second. At that pace it would take a few hundred thousand years to reach a distance where the naked eye could no longer pick it up, and well over a million before it slipped from view even through a modest telescope. Those are rough figures. Vectoring the star's known motion forward a few hundred thousand years puts it about forty-one light-years away. That's probably the nearest we'll ever come to a firm number.

So it's visible now, and it will stay visible for a very long time. It's not on any path to cross our orbit, strike us, or fall into the Sun. The only thing that could change that picture is a companion we haven't found yet. If Vega were pulling on something massive and unseen, its track across the sky would bend, and astronomers measure that track very precisely. Nobody has seen such a bend.

The other way it can fade is by burning out. Vega is a white main-sequence star about three and a half times the mass of the Sun, and stars that heavy live only a few hundred million years. Our Sun is about halfway through its own life. When Vega runs out of fuel it will swell into a red giant, brighten a good deal, and then settle as a white dwarf. So the sky will lose it twice: first as it drifts away, and much later as it dies.

As for whether anyone will be around to look up, that depends on Earth, and Earth has its own clock. Whether it's still here in a few hundred thousand years is a fair thing to wonder about, and I don't think anyone can give you a better answer than that.

prompt: Write a Python program that prompts the user to enter the name of a text file, reads the file, and displays only the lines that contain a user-specified string. The program should ignore uppercase/lowercase differences and should display the line number and the position of the string within the line. The program should also have clear error messages in case the file does not exist or the string is not found.
completion:
Here's a program that does what you asked for. I've added a few things that are worth knowing about.

```python
import os

def search_in_file():
    # Get the file name from the user
    file_name = input("Enter the name of the text file: ").strip()
    if not file_name:
        print("Error: No file name entered.")
        return

    # Read the file
    try:
        with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            lines = f.readlines()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: The file '{file_name}' does not exist.")
        return
    except PermissionError:
        print(f"Error: You do not have permission to read '{file_name}'.")
        return
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"Error reading '{file_name}': {e}")
        return

    # Get the search string from the user
    search = input("Enter the string to search for: ").strip()
    if not search:
        print("Error: No search string entered.")
        return

    # Convert to lower case once, so we compare lower case with lower case
    search_lower = search.lower()

    # Search through the lines
    found = False
    for line_number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        line_lower = line.lower()
        position = line_lower.find(search_lower)
        if position != -1:
            found = True
            # Show the line number, and the position of the first match
            print(f"Line {line_number}, position {position}: {line.rstrip()}")

    # Tell the user if nothing matched
    if not found:
        print(f"No lines containing '{search}' were found in '{file_name}'.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    search_in_file()
```

How it works. The file gets read once into memory, which is fine for normal text files. If you expect something very large, say a few gigabytes, it will use a lot of RAM, and a version that reads the file in chunks would be better. I've kept it simple here.

I've also gone a bit further than you asked. The program now asks for the search string, so you don't have to hard-code it. That makes it a useful little tool rather than a one-off script. It also shows the position of the match inside each line, and it tells you plainly if nothing was found.

One thing to know. The file is read with UTF-8 encoding. Some older Windows text files are in a different encoding, usually "latin-1" or "cp1252". If your files are like that, change the encoding argument, or remove it so Python picks up the system default.

Here is a version that doesn't ask for the string, in case you'd rather pass it on the command line:

```python
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    print("Usage: python search.py <file> <string>")
    sys.exit(1)

file_name, search = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]

try:
    with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line_number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
            if search.lower() in line.lower():
                print(f"Line {line_number}: {line.rstrip()}")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: The file '{file_name}' does not exist.")
except OSError as e:
    print(f"Error reading '{file_name}': {e}")
```

This version doesn't show the position of the match, because `in` doesn't give you that. If you want the position as well, replace the `if` line with the `find` check from the first version.

Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.
completion:
Since I can't put actual photos or videos in this guide, I've marked where a picture would help, with a short note on what you should be looking for. At the end are two short scripts you can film on your phone, or search for, to show the steps that depend on sight more than numbers.

What makes a good pancake is simple. The flour, the liquid and the egg come together into a batter that isn't overmixed. Everything else in this guide protects that.

What you'll need

The batter:
- 1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
- 2 teaspoons baking powder
- 2 tablespoons sugar
- ¼ teaspoon salt
- 1 large egg
- 1 cup (240 ml) milk, plus a little extra if the batter looks wrong
- 2 tablespoons melted butter, plus more for the pan
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract (optional)

The pan:
- A heavy skillet or non-stick frying pan, 10 to 12 inches
- A spatula, preferably thin and wide
- A jug or bowl with a spout for pouring
- A whisk, or a fork if you don't have one
- A small bowl and a spoon for mixing
- A thermometer, optional but useful

Step 1. Mix the dry ingredients
Put the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt into the small bowl. Whisk them together for about half a minute. The salt and the sugar are small, so measure them carefully. Too little salt and the pancakes taste flat. Too much and they taste salty all round.

Step 2. Add the wet ingredients
Make a well in the centre of the dry mix. Crack the egg into it, then pour in the milk, the melted butter and the vanilla. The butter should be melted, not hot. If it's hot, it will cook the egg a little, and you'll end up with little rubbery strands in your batter.

Step 3. Mix gently
Stir just until the flour is moistened. Lumps are fine. In fact, you want them. Mix it too much and the pancakes turn out tough and chewy. Think of it as mixing until it looks done, then stopping. This is the most important step in the whole recipe.

Step 4. Rest the batter
Leave it alone for about ten minutes. You'll see bubbles form on the surface and some of the lumps will settle. While the batter rests, melt a little more butter and get the pan ready.

Step 5. Heat the pan
Put the skillet over medium heat. Add a small knob of butter and swirl it around. If it foams and browns in under a minute, the pan is too hot. Turn the heat down. If the butter sits there solid, it's too cold. You want it to foam gently and stay pale gold. Drop a tiny spoonful of batter into the centre. It should sizzle and start to set within about half a minute. If it browns in ten seconds, the pan is too hot.

Step 6. Pour
Pour about ¼ cup of batter for each pancake, leaving a little space between them. Don't try to spread the batter. Let it settle into a round on its own. A ladle or a jug with a spout makes this easy.

Step 7. The first flip
Watch the surface. When bubbles form all over and most of them pop and leave a small hole, the edges will look set and dry, and the bottom will be golden, flip it. That takes about 1 to 2 minutes on the first side. Flip once, and only once. If you try to flip before the bubbles set, the pancake will tear.

Step 8. The second side
Cook the second side for about a minute, until it's golden. Then move it to a warm plate and keep the cooked pancakes in a low oven, covered with foil. The first ones will be the hottest and the last ones the coolest.

Step 9. Clean the pan between batches
Butter the pan again before each pancake, and wipe it clean with a little paper towel first. Burnt bits from the last pancake will stick to the next one.

Step 10. Serve
Serve straight away, while the edges are still crisp. Toppings are a matter of taste. Butter, syrup, fruit, yoghurt or a dusting of sugar all work.

Consistency: what to watch for

If the batter is too thick, it won't spread. You'll end up with small, dense rounds. Add milk a tablespoon at a time and stir gently.

If it's too thin, it will run all over the pan before it sets. Add a little flour, a tablespoon at a time.

If the pancakes climb the sides of the pan in a ring, the pan is too hot. Turn the heat down.

If they stay pale and never set, the heat is too low.

A thick batter cooks through more easily, so if you're unsure, aim for the thicker side.

A note on the milk: in many places milk is sold pasteurised, and a raw egg in a bowl is about as safe as it gets. If you're serving young children, older people, or anyone unwell, use pasteurised eggs, or cook the batter until it's set through. On the second side, cook it a little longer. If you'd rather not use raw egg at all, you can leave it out and add another tablespoon of milk. The pancakes will be a little less rich and a little less puffy, and that's fine.

Other safety points: the pan handle will get hot, so turn it towards the back of the stove and keep the spatula handle pointing the same way, where nobody's arm has to go. Melted butter in a hot pan can splatter, so add it carefully and step back a little. And don't pour water on a pan that's smoking.

Video guide, if you'd rather watch than read

If you'd like a video to go with this, two short clips will cover most of it.

The first clip, forty seconds or so, covers mixing and resting. Film the dry ingredients going in, then the egg cracking into the well, then the whisk moving through the batter just until it looks done, with the lumps still there. Show the clock at ten minutes. Show the bubbles coming up through the lumps. That's what you're looking for on every batch.

The second clip, about thirty seconds, covers the flip. Film the batter hitting the pan, then a time-lapse of the bubbles forming and popping. When the edges look dry, lift one up with the spatula to show the golden colour, then flip it.

Search for "how to make pancakes from scratch" and you'll find plenty of good ones. Some are only a minute or two long, which is enough. If you tell me who will be cooking, I can make the steps shorter and simpler, or add a few more.

prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner is a small piece of work that pays for itself. It is drawn by the app itself, usually with the app's own colours and shape, and it appears in the place where the content is about to show. Three things follow from that.

Visual design. A spinner that matches the app's style makes the wait feel like part of the app. A system icon in a different colour, with a different shape, tells the user they have left the app and entered the operating system's generic waiting state. Consistency matters here. If every screen of your app uses the same spinner, the user learns what it means, and a familiar symbol is read faster than a new one.

Loading time. This is the part people get wrong, so it is worth saying plainly. A custom spinner does not make the content load faster. The time it takes to fetch the data is the time it takes. What it can do is make the wait feel shorter. A pleasant, familiar animation is easier to sit through than a blank screen or a flashing cursor. There is also a practical gain. A spinner can sit in the space the content will occupy, so when the data arrives the app does not have to jump around to fit it in. That is a real reduction in the time the user spends shifting their eyes, and it is often noticed even though nobody measures it.

Interactive experience. A spinner tells the user two things at once. It tells them the app is working, so they do not click the button again, and it tells them roughly how long to wait. That second part matters most when the wait is long. If the content will take more than a few seconds, show the spinner and say so, for example "Loading your messages, this may take a moment." A spinner by itself says nothing about length, and the user's guesses tend toward the worst case.

There is one tradeoff, and it is mostly about space. A spinner has to live somewhere. If it sits on top of the content, the user cannot see what is coming. That is fine for a list that is about to appear. It is a poor choice when the layout is already crowded and the content is short, because the user has to wait to read it and cannot judge from a glance how long the wait will be. In that case a smaller indicator, or a line that says how many items are loading, may serve them better.

One more point. The user cannot control the spinner, and they should not have to. Do not put a refresh button inside it or make it possible to close. When the state is clear and fixed, the user stops checking and relaxes. When it seems open, they keep looking at it and clicking around it. A spinner that cannot be dismissed is doing its job.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
Google Search Console (GSC) shows how a site performs in Google Search: which queries bring people in, which pages get seen, and what's stopping Google from reading the site properly. This guide uses the current interface. Some older accounts still show the classic view, which works the same way but looks different. Where the two differ, I'll say so.

Before you start, make sure you own the site or have access to its account. You'll need a Google account, and for some sites a second account: if the site runs on WordPress.com or Blogger, your account there may already hold the site.

### Step 1: Add a property

1. Go to https://search.google.com/search-console and sign in.
2. Click "Add property" at the top left.
3. Type the full site address, including https://, and click "Add property".

Enter the exact address that visitors see. If your site is https://example.com, add it as https://example.com, not as example.com. GSC treats them as two different properties, and data can arrive slowly or not at all for the one you didn't enter.

If you already have a property for http://example.com, don't add https:// as a new one. Open the existing property and change the address in Settings, under "Property settings". Otherwise you'll have two properties spliting the same traffic.

### Step 2: Verify ownership

GSC needs to know the site is yours before it shows data. Click "Verify", then choose a method. I'll rank them.

1. DNS record (Domain property). If you can add a TXT record to your domain's DNS, do that. It covers the domain and all its subdomains, and it stays valid when you change hosts. It's the most durable check there is.
2. HTML file upload. Download the verification file from GSC and upload it to your site's root, so it sits at https://example.com/google[xxxx].html. Then click "Verify".
3. Meta tag. Copy the meta tag GSC gives you and paste it into your site's head section, then click "Verify".
4. Google Analytics. If the GA4 account is owned by the same person and the site already carries the GA4 tag, you can verify through it. I'd check that the tag is actually on the live site first. If it isn't, this method verifies nothing.
5. Google Tag Manager. Possible, but I'd skip it here and use the HTML file.

If verification fails, check that you typed the address exactly right in Step 1, and that the file or tag is live, not sitting in a draft.

Once verified, GSC shows a short confirmation message. Some data needs a few days to start arriving.

### Step 3: Understand the layout

The left menu has the main sections:

- Home: an overview of clicks, impressions, position and the top queries and pages.
- Pages: how each URL on your site is doing.
- Search appearance: how titles and meta descriptions look in search, and whether Google thinks they're good.
- Sitemaps: which sitemaps you've submitted and how many URLs they contain.
- Security and manual actions: penalties, hacked content and other policy issues.
- Settings: email notifications, user access and the property itself.

At the top of most pages is a date range picker. Set it to the last 3 months and check "Compare with previous period". That gives you a running baseline, which matters more than any single number.

### Step 4: Monitor search queries and pages

Go to "Search results", then to the "Queries" tab.

This table lists the searches that brought visitors to your site. Columns include the query, how many clicks it got, how many impressions, the click-through rate and the average position.

To see which pages rank for which queries, click "Pages" above the table. Now each row is a URL on your site, and you can see the queries it ranks for.

On the left, set the filter:

- Query contains: type a phrase to find every page that ranks for it.
- Page: type a path, such as /blog/, to see one section at a time.
- Country: search only for one place.
- Search type: web, image, video or news.

Copy the table to a spreadsheet whenever you want to keep a record. GSC doesn't keep old query data once you change the date range, so a monthly snapshot is worth keeping.

If you're checking one page's ranking for a specific keyword, use the URL inspection tool. Type the full address into the search box at the top of the page and hit enter. The report shows the live result, including whether the page ranks for the term right now. Enter one URL at a time.

### Step 5: Analyze clicks and impressions

Every page in GSC has an "Actions" menu with "Compare with other sites" and "Export". Click "Compare with other sites".

This tool lets you set up to four properties side by side. Add your own site and a competitor's, and GSC draws both on the same graph. You can compare clicks, impressions, position and CTR, for the whole site or for selected pages. It's the best thing in GSC for seeing how you're doing against someone else.

Two things to keep in mind. GSC only shows traffic from Google Search, not from other search engines, and not from social media or direct visits. That's most of search traffic for most sites, but not all of it. And impressions are rough. If a visitor opens a result and closes it quickly, GSC counts it as a click, so CTR is better as a trend than as an exact number.

### Step 6: Identify crawl errors

Go to "Pages", then to the "Not indexed" tab. This list is the most useful thing in GSC for finding what's breaking your site.

Click each status to expand it. Common problems:

- "Crawled, currently not indexed". Google read the page and chose not to index it. If you expect it to be in search, look at the page itself. Is the content thin? Is there another version of it on the site?
- "Duplicate, submitted URL not selected by Google". You told Google this page matters, and it picked another version. Usually you fix this by putting a canonical tag on the duplicate, pointing to the one you want.
- "Submitted URL marked as noindex". The page has a noindex tag on it, or in a sitemap or robot.txt file, and it's in a sitemap. Remove the tag or take the sitemap out.
- "Crawl error". The server failed when Google tried to read the page. That's a server problem, and it's worth reporting to whoever runs the site.

Click "Inspect" on any URL to see the live result for that page.

Don't panic over a few errors. A small site with a few hundred pages can easily have a few hundred "Crawled, not indexed" entries, most of them old posts nobody visits any more. Mark it as "Not a problem" when you've checked it. That clears it from the list and keeps a record of your check.

### Step 7: Submit sitemaps

Go to "Sitemaps". In "Add a new sitemap", type the path to your sitemap, usually /sitemap.xml, and click "Submit".

GSC also lists sitemaps it found on its own. If yours is missing from that list, the path is probably wrong, or Google hasn't found it yet.

If you changed the sitemap, or fixed pages that were blocked, click "Request indexing" from the URL inspection tool on the new or changed pages. That puts them in the queue sooner. It doesn't promise anything.

You can submit several sitemaps, including ones for images, video and news. Each one counts separately.

### Step 8: Set up email notifications

Go to "Settings", then to "Email notifications". Turn on the switches you want. I'd turn on all of them. You hear about a problem best before anyone else does, and a broken page costs a site nothing to fix.

Under "Site ownership", there's an option to email anyone who edits the property. Turn it on, and add the people who work on the site. Then if someone changes the sitemap or adds a noindex tag, the whole team finds out by email.

### Step 9: Give others access

In Settings, under "Users and permissions", you can add people by their email address. Give them "Owner" access only to people who should be able to delete the property or remove others. For most editors, "Reader" is enough. Readers can see everything, including the verification records, so they can't be locked out by someone who changes the access.

### Common problems

- No data after a week. Most often this means the wrong property, http:// versus https://. Check the address in Settings.
- Verification fails every time you change hosting. A DNS record doesn't depend on the host, so it's the one check that survives a move.
- A sudden fall in clicks. Look first at "Security and manual actions", then at "Not indexed". A penalty or a bulk noindex is the usual cause.
- Too many results to read. Filter by date, by country and by page, and export to a spreadsheet.

If your site uses a platform like WordPress, a plugin can put the verification meta tag on your site and send you the GSC reports by email. That's a personal choice. The steps above work without one.

If the interface has changed since this was written, look for the same labels in the menu. Most of them haven't moved in years.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. Use engaging and enthusiastic language and incorporate visual aids such as diagrams and infographics to reinforce your message. Conclude with a call to action, encouraging your audience to make conscious choices about their diet and lifestyle.
completion:
Ladies and gentlemen, friends, colleagues,

Look at the plate in front of you. Now look at the one next to it. One is a sandwich, some chips, a soda. The other is a bowl of colour: greens, a protein, something bright like peppers or carrots or fruit. Both will get you through the afternoon. Only one of them will still be doing good for you at four o'clock.

I want to persuade you today that what you eat matters more than you think, and less than you fear. Most of what goes wrong with our health is not one bad meal. It is the same choice made a thousand times, without thinking. And the good news is that a better choice can be simple.

Start with what the evidence tells us. In 2021 the Lancet published a study of nearly 195,000 people across nineteen countries, and the picture was plain. The people who ate the most ultra-processed foods had the worst health. The people who ate the most protein, fibre and vegetables had the best. The difference was large, and it held across every country in the study, rich and poor alike.

Then there is the heart, and the numbers here are about as good as health statistics get. In 1985 the New England Journal of Medicine reported on the Lyon Diet Heart Study. People who had survived a heart attack were put on either a normal hospital diet or a Mediterranean one, with more fish, more vegetables, olive oil instead of butter, and less red meat. By the fifth month, the recurrence of heart problems in the experimental group had fallen by more than half. The doctors stopped the trial early because the normal diet was clearly doing worse.

And it is not only the heart. A large review in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2019 found that people who followed a Mediterranean-style diet had a substantially lower risk of dying from any cause than those who did not.

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. "I have no time." "My children will only eat chicken nuggets." "I have tried before and fallen off." Let me answer each one.

Time. The people who eat well are usually not the ones who cook from nothing every evening. They are the ones who planned on a Sunday for about an hour. So plan. Once a week, sit down with your calendar. Any evening with a meeting or a late session is one evening you will not cook. Buy for those nights in advance: frozen vegetables, tinned fish, a roast chicken. On the other evenings, cook once and eat twice. Make pasta sauce on Wednesday and it is lunch on Thursday.

Do not make the whole week your enemy. Start with one day. Eat well on one day of the week, and make that day so easy that you can do it again.

The children. Children have to learn what a carrot is, just as they had to learn what a spoon is. They are still working it out. Give them a small piece of something new alongside the food they already eat, and do not take the rest away as a punishment. And you decide what goes on the table. They decide how much they eat. Parents who worry most about their children's weight often end up controlling their eating most, and the children learn to eat in secret.

And falling off is not a disaster. It is a Tuesday. The next meal is always still coming.

Now imagine this. A man in his fifties, let us call him David, who had been told for years that he would always be tired after lunch. He had one rule. No soda, ever. Just water or tea. His energy did not come back all at once. By the third week he noticed that his afternoons had changed. By the fifth he had stopped reaching for the biscuit tin at three o'clock. He told me he had not felt that awake in twenty years.

And a woman I know, let us call her Priya. She started cooking again after her mother got sick. She told me it was not about her mother. It was about remembering what her grandmother's kitchen had smelled like. A year later she said she felt more like herself than she had in a long time.

These are two people. But they show the same thing: that food works on your body, your mind and your memory at once.

Visual aid: the plate. Half of your plate, vegetables and fruit. A quarter, protein: fish, chicken, eggs, beans, lentils, tofu. A quarter, starch: potatoes, rice, bread, pasta, chosen as often as not in their whole form. And water, most of the time.

Visual aid: the shopping list. Half of it should be the foods you eat every week. If your list is all surprises, you will buy surprises.

Visual aid: the timeline. A graph showing how risk falls as a habit holds, with the first week marked "nothing yet" and the third week marked "you notice."

Visual aid: the snack drawer. Put the good food where you can see it, at eye level, washed and cut. You will eat what is nearest.

Visual aid: the tiredness curve. A simple line showing energy after a heavy lunch and after a light one.

So here is my challenge to you. This week, change one thing. One drink, one day, one trip to the shop. And when you do it, tell someone. A friend, a colleague, the person next to you on the bus.

Your body is the only place you have to live. Food is the main thing that goes into it. You do not need a perfect diet. You need a better one than the one you are on now, and you need it to last.

Thank you.
